synteresis.etymology: From Medieval Latin *syntērēsis*, from Ancient Greek *συντήρησις* (“careful watching”), from *συντηρεῖν* (“to keep guard”).

senses.definition: In a systematic manner; organizedly or methodically.
senses.example: Taxonomy seeks to systematically name all living organisms; each species has one name and everyone can figure out what that name is.

core.definition: In an organized, step-by-step way, following a plan rather than acting at random.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAT. The ending is -ically, pronounced -ih-klee, with a short i and a clear k before the ly sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests thoroughness and discipline, and it is common in reports, research, and professional writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'systematically' when describing how someone checked, tested, or organized something. It is a bit more formal than 'step by step' or 'one by one.' In casual conversation, people often choose simpler words like 'carefully' or 'one thing at a time.'

distinctions.note: Carefully focuses on attention and caution, while systematically focuses on following an orderly plan.
Methodically and systematically are close in meaning, but methodically stresses a steady, deliberate pace.

examples.everyday: Let's go through the closet systematically so we don't miss anything.
examples.professional: The QA team systematically reproduced each bug before filing the ticket.
examples.analytical: The author systematically dismantles each objection, showing how every premise depends on the one before it.

nuance.analogy: Working systematically is like searching a house room by room with a flashlight, so no corner is left in the dark.
nuance.etymology: From systematic plus the adverbial ending -ally, from Greek sustēma, 'a whole put together.'
common_mistakes: Dropping the -ically ending and saying 'systematicly'; the correct spelling is systematically.
Confusing it with 'systemically,' which describes effects spread through a whole system.

senses.definition: To drive dangerously close behind another vehicle.
senses.example: If that idiot keeps tailgating our car they'll end up rear-endeding us.

senses.definition: To participate in a tailgate party.
senses.example: We planned to tailgate in the stadium parking lot before the football game.

senses.definition: To follow another person through access control on their access, rather than on one’s own credentials, especially when entering a door controlled by a card reader.
senses.example: Security experts warned that employees often tailgate colleagues through the lobby door.

senses.definition: To privately purchase or sell a security immediately after trading in the same security for a client.
senses.example: The compliance officer flagged the trader who tailgated personal purchases right after client orders.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of tailgate party.
senses.example: Are you coming to the tailgate? We'll be grilling brisket.

senses.definition: A hinged board or hatch at the rear of a vehicle that can be lowered for loading and unloading.
senses.example: Drop the tailgate, please, and I'll load these pallets.

senses.definition: The downstream gate in the lock on a canal or river, or in an irrigation system.
senses.example: The locktender closed the tailgate and the chamber started to fill.

senses.definition: A tunnel for drawing spent air away from the working face of a mine.
senses.example: Miners opened a tailgate to carry foul air away from the working face.

core.definition: To drive dangerously close behind another vehicle, leaving too little space to stop safely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TAIL, in both the noun and the verb. Say the final t clearly, and do not stress the second syllable as in gate-keeper style phrasing.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing driving. Americans use it as a complaint about unsafe drivers. The noun for a party before a game is cheerful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'You're tailgating me' to a driver who is too close behind them, often with a frustrated tone. The noun tailgate also means the hinged rear panel of a pickup truck, and a tailgate party is a major American custom before football games. Using the verb for a party is informal, so say 'We're going to tailgate before the game' among friends.

distinctions.note: Following is neutral and describes any distance behind a car; tailgate implies the distance is unsafe or rude.
Cutting off means changing lanes in front of someone; tailgating means driving too close behind them.

examples.everyday: Hey, back off a little, you're tailgating me in this rain.
examples.professional: Our security team reported someone tailgating through the side door of the lab, so please badge in with your own card.
examples.analytical: To tailgate in traffic is to shrink the margin of safety, whereas in access control it means exploiting another person's legitimate entry.

nuance.analogy: Like a rider drafting so closely behind a racer that he gets pulled along without any effort of his own.
nuance.etymology: From tail plus gate; the gate is the hinged board at the back of a wagon or truck.
common_mistakes: Using tailgate only for a party; in traffic, the verb means driving too close.
Stressing the second syllable, saying tail-GATE, instead of TAIL-gate.

conversation.text: Don't tailgate; you can't stop in time if he brakes.
The truck behind me tailgated me for ten miles.
We tailgate before every home game with burgers in the parking lot.
Put the cooler on the tailgate.
We're going to tailgate before the game. Want to come?
The tailgate starts at ten in the stadium parking lot.
Stop tailgating that car; you're way too close.

senses.definition: Adjusted by a tailor, fitted.
Made by a tailor.
senses.example: His expensive tailored shirts didn't look that much better than off-the-rack, but they lasted much longer.

core.definition: Made or adjusted to fit a particular person, need or purpose closely, especially a piece of clothing with a neat, fitted shape.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final -ed a single d sound after the r-colored syllable. Do not add an extra syllable as in 'TAY-ler-ed'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests neatness, polish and careful attention to detail.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tailored for suits, jackets and pants, and also for plans or responses that have been adjusted for a specific group. In clothing contexts it implies a clean, structured fit. Saying 'tailored' about a casual T-shirt would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Fitted means closely following the body's shape, while tailored implies skilled cutting and adjustment, often with a structured look.
Tailored emphasizes adjusting something to fit, while custom emphasizes that it was specially ordered or made.

examples.everyday: She wore a tailored navy jacket to her cousin's wedding and looked great.
examples.professional: Our sales team sends tailored proposals to each client, based on their industry and budget.
examples.analytical: Tailored arguments adjust claims to a particular audience's assumptions, which can clarify meaning while narrowing the scope of the claim.

nuance.analogy: A tailored garment is like a glove molded to one particular hand.
nuance.etymology: From tailor, from Old French taillier, to cut, plus the -ed ending.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an extra syllable, as in 'TAY-ler-ed'.
Using tailored for ready-to-wear clothes, when it means clothes made or adjusted to fit a person closely.

senses.definition: To swim.

core.definition: To swim briefly, usually in a pool, lake or ocean, for a quick cool-down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DIP. Keep the short i in dip, and in fast speech take a sounds like tay-kuh.

nuance.connotation: Positive and relaxed. It suggests a refreshing swim on a warm day.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use take a dip for a short, casual swim, especially on vacation or in summer. For a longer swim, say 'go for a swim'. A natural reply is 'Sounds great, I'll grab the towels.'

distinctions.note: Go for a swim is the usual phrase for a longer, more deliberate swim; take a dip is shorter and more casual.
Take a plunge can mean jumping into water boldly, or a risky financial commitment; take a dip is only about swimming.

collocations: take a dip in the lake
take a dip in the pool

examples.everyday: It's ninety degrees, let's take a dip in the lake before dinner.
examples.professional: After the offsite, a few of us took a dip in the hotel pool before the team dinner.
examples.analytical: The phrase relies on a metaphor of immersion, where a brief dip signals a temporary and partial contact with an element.

nuance.analogy: Like touching a toe into a lake to test it, then deciding to fully jump in.
nuance.etymology: Take from Old Norse taka; dip from Old English dyppan.
common_mistakes: Using take a dip for a long swim, when go for a swim is more natural.
Confusing dip with deep, which changes both the sound and the meaning.

conversation.text: It's so hot; let's take a dip in the lake.
I'm going to take a quick dip before dinner.
Do you want to take a dip, or are you staying on the beach?

senses.definition: To leave the ground and ascend into the air or into flight.
senses.example: The plane has been cleared to take off from runway 3.

senses.definition: To become successful, to flourish.
senses.example: The business has really taken off this year and has made quite a profit.

senses.definition: To remove.
senses.example: He took off his shoes.

senses.definition: To take (a specified time period) as a vacation or break from work or other activity.
senses.example: I'd like to take next Friday off to attend a wedding.

senses.definition: To absent oneself from work or other responsibility, especially with permission.
senses.example: If you take off for Thanksgiving you must work Christmas and vice versa.

senses.definition: To depart.
senses.example: I'm going to take off now.

senses.definition: To stand up on a surfboard and begin to surf a breaking wave.
senses.example: He waited for the right wave, then managed to take off and ride it all the way in.

senses.definition: To imitate (somebody), often in a satirical manner.
senses.example: Much of his act involves taking off the Prime Minister and other politicians.

senses.definition: To quantify.
senses.example: I'll take off the concrete and steel for this construction project.

senses.definition: (dated) To take drugs; to inject drugs.
senses.example: Back then, half the guys in the band would take off before every gig, honestly.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To steal (something) or rob (someone).
senses.example: Two masked men tried to take off the jewelry store before the alarm went off.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To remove clothing or an object, or for a plane to leave the ground, or to leave quickly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OFF, with a vowel close to 'caught'. In phrases, 'take off' links to 'tay-KAWF'. The t in 'take' is light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'take off' for removing shoes or jackets at home, for a plane leaving the runway, and for a business or product becoming popular. 'I'm taking off' means I'm leaving now, which is casual. In a restaurant, you can ask 'Can I take off the lid?'

distinctions.note: 'Remove' is more formal and general; 'take off' is conversational and often used for clothing.
'Leave' is neutral; 'take off' suggests suddenness or informality.

examples.everyday: Please take off your shoes when you come in, the floor was just cleaned.
examples.professional: Our startup really started to take off after the product launch in March.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that rational inquiry can take off from ordinary observation, rising like a plane from the runway of experience.

nuance.analogy: Like a plane lifting from the runway, a small effort can suddenly rise into success.
common_mistakes: Using 'take off' as a noun without a hyphen in formal writing; 'takeoff' is the standard noun.
Confusing 'take off' with 'take off of'; 'off of' is not standard.

conversation.text: Please take off your shoes before coming inside.
Our flight took off an hour late.
Her business really took off last year.
I'm going to take off now, see you tomorrow.
I'm taking Friday off to go fishing.
It's late, so I'm going to take off.
Take off your shoes at security.
Our flight takes off at six in the morning.

senses.definition: Talkative or loquacious.
Containing a great deal of dialogue or talking in general.
senses.example: The director's second cut was talky, with long conversations replacing most of the action.

core.definition: Talkative, or (of a film, play or book) containing too much dialogue and too little action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the vowel the 'aw' of 'caught'. The final -y is a clear 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative. Calling a movie or script 'talky' means it is boring, while calling a person 'talky' is somewhat rude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'talky' mainly to criticize films, plays, novels or presentations that rely too heavily on dialogue. For people, 'chatty' or 'talkative' is more common and gentler. Critics might say 'The first act is a little talky' to suggest it needs more action.

distinctions.note: Talkative describes a person who talks a lot, while talky describes a work with too much dialogue or, informally, a person who chatters too much.
Chatty is friendly and light, while talky is usually a criticism.

collocations: too talky for its own good

examples.everyday: My uncle gets so talky after a couple of beers that nobody else can get a word in.
examples.professional: The pitch deck is too talky; cut the bullet points and show the chart.
examples.analytical: The novel's talky middle section lets its characters argue theology at length while the plot stalls.

nuance.analogy: A talky film is like a meeting that could have been an email.
nuance.etymology: From talk plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using 'talky' as a compliment; it is usually negative
Confusing 'talky' with 'talkative' when describing a person

senses.definition: A conical peg or pin used to close and open the hole or vent in a container.
senses.example: The barrel's tap had worked loose, so cider leaked across the cellar floor.

senses.definition: An object with a tapering conical form like a tap (etymology 1, noun sense 1); specifically, ellipsis of taproot (“long, tapering root of a plant”).
senses.example: Dandelions survive droughts because their thick tap reaches deep into the soil.

senses.definition: A hollow device used to control the flow of a fluid, such as an alcoholic beverage from a cask, or a gas or liquid in a pipe.
senses.example: We don’t have bottled water; you’ll have to get it from the tap.

senses.definition: Liquor drawn through a tap (etymology 1, noun sense 2.2); hence, a certain kind or quality of liquor; also, a certain kind or quality of any thing.
senses.example: a liquor of the same tap

senses.definition: A device used to listen in secretly on telephone calls or other communications.
senses.example: Investigators found a tap on the suspect's phone line after months of surveillance.

senses.definition: A secret interception of telephone calls or other communications using such a device; also, a recording of such a communication.
senses.example: telephone tap

senses.definition: A situation where a borrowing government authority issues bonds over a period of time, usually at a fixed price, with volumes sold on a particular day dependent on market conditions.
senses.example: bond tap tap issue

senses.definition: A cylindrical tool used to cut an internal screw thread in a hole, with cutting edges around the lower end and an upper end to which a handle is fitted to turn the tool.
senses.example: We drilled a hole and then cut the threads with the proper tap to match the valve’s thread.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of taphouse or taproom (“place where alcoholic beverages are served on tap”).
A light blow or strike with a clear sound; a gentle rap; a pat; also, the sound made by such a blow or strike.
senses.example: When Steve felt a tap on his shoulder, he turned around.

senses.definition: The smallest amount of work; a stroke of work.
senses.example: Give the chapter one last tap before we send it to the editor.

senses.definition: One of the metal pieces attached to the sole of a tap dancer's shoe at the toe and heel to cause a tapping sound.
senses.example: The dancer's taps echoed loudly off the wooden stage during the final number.

senses.definition: A shot fired from a firearm.
senses.example: Witnesses heard a single tap from the rooftop before the officer fell.

senses.definition: An act of touching a button, icon, or specific location on the touch screen of an electronic device such as a mobile phone to invoke a function.
senses.example: Just give the app icon a quick tap to open your account settings.

senses.definition: A single muscle contraction in vocal organs causing a consonant sound; also, the sound so made.
senses.example: The English t in butter is often realized as a flap, a quick tap of the tongue.

senses.definition: A piece of leather or other material fastened upon the bottom of an item of footwear when repairing the heel or sole; also the sole of an item of footwear.
senses.example: The cobbler replaced the worn tap on my boots, so they grip the pavement better.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of tap dance.
A procedure that removes fluid from a body cavity; paracentesis.
senses.example: abdominal tap pleural tap spinal tap

senses.definition: To furnish (a container, etc.) with a tap (noun etymology 1, noun sense 2.2) so that liquid can be drawn.
senses.example: The brewer tapped the new keg on Friday so customers could pour pints.

senses.definition: To draw off (a liquid) from a container or other source; also, to draw off a liquid from (a container or other source).
senses.example: He tapped the ten-year-old whiskey from its barrel.

senses.definition: To break into or open up (a thing) so as to obtain something; to exploit, to penetrate; tap into.
senses.example: Businesses are trying to tap the youth market.

senses.definition: To deplete (something); to tap out.
senses.example: The company tapped its emergency fund to cover the unexpected repairs.

senses.definition: To ask or beg for (something) to be given for free; to cadge, to scrounge; also, to ask or beg (someone) to give something for free.
senses.example: I tried to tap a cigarette off him, but he wouldn’t give me one.

senses.definition: To turn over (a playing card or playing piece) to remind players that it has already been used in that round.
senses.example: In the game, she tapped the used card to signal that it had already been played.

senses.definition: To force (an opponent) to place all their poker chips in the pot (that is, to go all in) by wagering all of one's own chips.
senses.example: Desperate, he tapped everything on a pair of fours and lost the hand.

senses.definition: To remove a taproot from (a plant).
senses.example: The landscaper tapped the old oak stump to clear every root before grading the lot.

senses.definition: To cut an internal screw thread in (a hole); also, to cut (an internal screw thread) in a hole, or to create an internally threaded hole in (something).
senses.example: Tap an M3 thread all the way through the hole.

senses.definition: To cut an external screw thread into (a bolt or rod) to create a screw.
senses.example: The machinist tapped the steel rod so the nut could screw onto it.

senses.definition: To put (a screw or other object) in or through another thing.
senses.example: I tapped two screws into the drywall to hang the new shelf.

senses.definition: To act as a tapster; to draw an alcoholic beverage from a container.
To strike (someone or something), chiefly lightly with a clear sound, but sometimes hard.
senses.example: Emma tapped Jim on the shoulder to get his attention.

senses.definition: Also in the form tap on the shoulder: to arrest (someone).
To have sexual intercourse with (someone).
senses.example: I would tap that hot girl over there.

senses.definition: To shoot (someone or something) with a firearm.
To (lightly) touch (a finger, foot, or other body part) on a surface, often repeatedly.
senses.example: You can pay by tapping your card.

senses.definition: To lightly touch a touchscreen, usually an icon or button, to activate a function.
senses.example: Next, tap on the browser to get on the internet.

senses.definition: To lightly and repeatedly touch (a person or one or more body parts) as part of various forms of psychological treatment.
senses.example: The therapist tapped him when he was overcome by anxiety.

senses.definition: To invoke a function on an electronic device such as a mobile phone by touching (a button, icon, or specific location on its touch screen).
To repair (an item of footwear) by putting on a new heel or sole, or a piece of material on to the heel or sole.
senses.example: to tap shoes

senses.definition: To choose or designate (someone) for a duty, an honor, membership of an organization, or a position.
senses.example: He was tapped by the president to act as a special counsel.

senses.definition: Often followed by at or on: to strike lightly with a clear sound; also, to make a sharp noise through this action.
senses.example: The tree was swaying in the breeze and tapping on the window pane.

senses.definition: To walk by striking the ground lightly with a clear sound.
Of a bell, a drum, etc.: to make a sharp noise, often as a signal.
To drain off fluid from (a person or a body cavity) by paracentesis.

To connect a listening and/or recording device to (a communication cable or device) in order to listen in secretly on telephone calls or other communications; also, to secretly listen in on and/or record (a telephone call or other communication).
senses.example: They can’t tap the phone without a warrant.

senses.definition: To force (an opponent) to submit, chiefly by indicating their intention to do so by striking a hand on the ground several times; to tap out.
To submit to an opponent, chiefly by indicating an intention to do so by striking a hand on the ground several times; to tap out.

core.definition: A faucet or valve that controls the flow of water, beer or another liquid from a pipe, sink or keg.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short a as in cat, not the long a of tape. The final p is usually unreleased in casual speech, so it sounds almost like tap-with-a-stop.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is ordinary and carries no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tap mainly for water supply, as in tap water, and for beer or draft taps in bars. For a sink or bathtub fixture, most Americans say faucet, and tap sounds British in that sense. Ordering tap water or asking for a beer on tap is entirely natural.

distinctions.note: Faucet is the standard American word for a sink, tub or wall fixture, while tap is more common for water supply and beer dispensers.
A spigot is usually an outdoor or barrel valve, often attached to a garden hose or a large container.
Valve is a technical term for any device controlling flow, while tap is a more everyday, specific word for dispensing a liquid.

examples.everyday: Can you turn off the tap? It's been dripping all night.
examples.professional: The brewery's new tap system lets the bartenders pour six beers at the same time.
examples.analytical: Water from the tap is only as clean as the pipes that carry it, so the source matters as much as the spout.

nuance.analogy: A tap is like a gate in a dam: it stays closed until you open it, and then the flow depends on how far you turn it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tæppa, meaning plug or spigot.
common_mistakes: Saying tap for a bathroom or kitchen sink fixture, which sounds British; Americans say faucet there.
Pronouncing it with a long a as in tape.

tap.etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English *tappe* (“hollow device for controlling the flow of liquid from a hole, cock, faucet, spigot; hole through which the liquid flows; the liquid which thus flows”), from Old English *tæppa*, from **tappō*, from…

senses.definition: In a tedious or wearisome manner.

core.definition: In a way that is long, slow, and boring, so that it tires or annoys you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. Keep the middle syllables short and weak, and end with a light 'lee' rather than a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes how something is done, usually with a sense of wearying slowness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tediously mostly in writing or formal speech to describe a slow process, as in 'The repairs proceeded tediously.' In everyday speech people more often say 'it took forever' or 'it was a slog.' It is rarely used to mean 'tiresomely rude' about a person.

distinctions.note: Slowly only describes speed; tediously adds that the slowness is boring or wearying.
Laboriously stresses great effort and hard work, while tediously stresses dullness and repetition.

examples.everyday: The line at the post office moved tediously, so I almost gave up.
examples.professional: The migration script ran tediously because it processed each record one at a time.
examples.analytical: The author tediously repeats the same distinction across three chapters without advancing the argument.

nuance.analogy: Tediously is like a slow song played at half speed: you can follow it, but every note drags.
nuance.etymology: Formed from tedious with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'tediously' to describe a person's character rather than a process.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural to American ears.

core.definition: A town in the hills of Judah, about ten miles south of Bethlehem, known as the home of the prophet Amos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'KOH'. Finish with a soft 'uh' rather than a hard 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name used in biblical and historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mention Tekoa mainly in Bible study, sermons, or history talks. Pronounce the place name the same way in conversation, and say 'the town of Tekoa' if you need to clarify. It is not a common word in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Tekoa refers to the town, while Tekoite refers to a person from it, such as Amos.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study read about Amos, and someone asked where Tekoa is.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, I placed Tekoa in Judah to show that the prophet spoke from outside the northern kingdom.
examples.analytical: Amos's self-description as a herdsman of Tekoa, in 1:1, shapes how readers understand his prophetic authority.

nuance.analogy: Tekoa is like a hometown mentioned in a story: it tells you where the speaker came from and why his voice carries an outsider's edge.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew tĕqoaʿ, a place name in Judah.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in TEK-oh-uh.
Pronouncing the final vowel as a hard 'ah' rather than a soft 'uh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Tekoa (Hebrew tĕqoaʿ) was a town in the hill country of Judah, about ten miles south of Jerusalem's neighbor Bethlehem, known for its shepherds and its wilderness. It is the hometown of the prophet Amos, who calls himself a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs (Amos 7:14). In 2 Samuel 14:2 Joab sends a wise woman from Tekoa to speak to King David, and in 2 Chronicles 11:6 King Rehoboam fortifies Tekoa among the cities of Judah. Jeremiah 6:1 also calls for a trumpet to be blown in Tekoa, a sign of warning.

senses.definition: Mental senses related to determining, reckoning, or perceiving.
senses.example: All told, there were over a dozen. Can you tell time on a clock? He had untold wealth.

senses.definition: To notice, discern. (Roughly, "can tell" means "know" but with a sense of direct perception.)
senses.example: I can tell that you're thrilled.

senses.definition: To pick up on a difference. (See tell apart for more.)
senses.example: An expert can tell an original from a forgery.

senses.definition: Social senses of communicating.
senses.example: I want to tell a story; I want to tell you a story.

senses.definition: To narrate, to recount.
senses.example: I want to tell a story; I want to tell you a story.

senses.definition: To convey by speech; to say.
senses.example: Finally, someone told him the truth. He seems to like to tell lies.

senses.definition: To instruct or inform.
senses.example: Please tell me how to do it.

senses.definition: To order; to direct, to say to someone.
senses.example: Tell him to go away.

senses.definition: To use (beads or similar objects) as an aid to prayer.
senses.example: Every evening my grandmother would tell her rosary beads as she prayed quietly by the window.

senses.definition: To inform someone in authority about a wrongdoing.
senses.example: I saw you steal those sweets! I'm telling!

senses.definition: To reveal information in prose through outright expository statement — contrasted with show.
senses.example: Maria rewrote the section of her novel that talked about Meg and Sage's friendship to have less telling and more showing.

senses.definition: Abstract senses related to showing or revealing To reveal.
senses.example: Time will tell what became of him.

senses.definition: To show, be showing, be revealed.
senses.example: The tree rings began to tell a story of droughts that lasted several years.

senses.definition: To reveal.
senses.example: Time will tell what became of him.

senses.definition: To have an effect, especially a noticeable one; to be apparent, to be demonstrated.
senses.example: Sir Gerald was moving slower; his wounds were beginning to tell.

senses.definition: (of a fact) To support a certain position.
senses.example: The new survey data tells strongly in favor of raising the minimum wage.

senses.definition: A reflexive, often habitual behavior, especially one occurring in a context that often features attempts at deception by persons under psychological stress (such as a poker game or police interrogation), that reveals information that the person exhibiting the behavior is attempting to withhold.
senses.example: The player's tell was rubbing his ear whenever he was bluffing with weak cards.

senses.definition: A giveaway; something that unintentionally reveals or hints at a secret.
senses.example: Her tell was the way she checked her phone whenever she lied about working late.

senses.definition: A private message to an individual in a chat room; a whisper.
senses.example: Jordan sent me a tell in the chat room asking if I wanted to talk privately.

senses.definition: A hill or mound, originally and especially in the Middle East, over or consisting of the ruins of ancient settlements.
senses.example: The archaeologists dug into the tell, uncovering layers of pottery from three different ancient cities.

core.definition: To give someone information in words, or to say something to them so they know it.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'eh' vowel, as in 'bed', not the long 'ay' of 'tail'. End with a clear 'l' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an everyday, flexible verb.
nuance.usage_note: 'Tell' is one of the most common verbs in American speech, used constantly in casual conversation. Americans say 'tell me' with the object directly after the verb, and they avoid 'tell to me'. Often 'tell' introduces a statement, as in 'Tell him I said hi.'

distinctions.note: 'Say' focuses on the words spoken, while 'tell' requires a person who receives the information ('tell me' rather than 'say me').
'Inform' is formal and official, while 'tell' is everyday.
'Speak' focuses on the act of talking, while 'tell' focuses on conveying information or a story.

examples.everyday: Can you tell me how to get to the store on Main Street?
examples.professional: Please tell the team about the schedule change before Thursday's standup.
examples.analytical: Augustine asks what it means to tell the truth about one's inner life, and whether confession can be honest without self-deception.

nuance.analogy: Telling is like handing someone a package: the information passes from your hands into theirs.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tellan 'to count, relate, recount'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tell to me' instead of 'tell me'.
Using 'say' with a person as object, as in 'He said me the news'; use 'tell' instead.

tell.etymology: From Middle English *tellen* (“to count, tell”), from Old English *tellan* (“to count, tell”), from **talljan*, from Proto-Germanic **taljaną*, **talzijaną* (“to count, enumerate”), from Proto-Germanic **talą*, **talō* (“number, counting”), from…

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see tell,‎ truth.
senses.example: Please tell the truth, even if the answer disappoints your mother.

senses.definition: Used to positively assert the frank honesty of an associated statement of set of statements; equivalent to "to tell the truth".
senses.example: I didn't enjoy the film, to tell the truth, though everyone else loved it.

core.definition: To say only what is true, without lying, hiding facts or leaving out important details.

pronunciation.tip: 'The' reduces to 'thuh' before a consonant. Keep the r in 'truth' and end with a voiceless 'th' sound, not an 'f'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can sound pointed or suspicious when used as a demand, as in 'Just tell me the truth.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tell the truth' in everyday talk and in courts, where witnesses swear to 'tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth'. Casual speakers often add 'to tell you the truth' before sharing an honest opinion. A natural reply is 'Thanks for being honest with me.'

distinctions.note: 'Be honest' is a more casual request, while 'tell the truth' can sound more serious or even accusatory.
'Level with someone' is informal and means to speak candidly about a situation, often after avoiding it.
'Say the truth' is unnatural in American English; 'tell the truth' is the standard phrase.

examples.everyday: To tell you the truth, I'd rather stay home and watch a movie tonight.
examples.professional: I need you to tell the truth about the delay so we can fix the timeline before the client call.
examples.analytical: Scripture and philosophy both ask whether a person can tell the truth when honesty costs social standing.

nuance.analogy: It's like wiping a window clean so that light passes through without distortion.
nuance.etymology: 'Tell' is from Old English tellan; 'truth' is from Old English trēowth, meaning faithfulness.
common_mistakes: Saying 'say the truth' instead of 'tell the truth'.
Dropping 'the' in casual speech and saying 'tell truth', which sounds incomplete.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Greek New Testament, truth is alētheia, meaning reality or what is real and dependable, and the verb aletheuein means to speak or live truly. Ephesians 4:25 tells believers to put away falsehood and speak the truth with their neighbors, because they are members of one another. Ephesians 4:15 speaks of speaking the truth in love. Psalm 15:2 describes the person who speaks truth from the heart.

senses.definition: A person who tells stories.
senses.example: My grandfather was a gifted teller who kept the whole family laughing at dinner.

senses.definition: A bank clerk who receives and pays out money.
A cashier at any place of business.
senses.example: The teller counted out my twenties and asked whether I wanted a receipt.

senses.definition: Synonym of automated teller machine.
senses.example: The nearest teller is out of order, so I'll use the one by the gas station.

senses.definition: A person who counts the votes in an election.
senses.example: The teller announced the final tally after counting every ballot twice.

core.definition: A bank employee who receives deposits and pays out cash to customers at a window or drive-through.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light, r-colored schwa, not a long 'ur' or 'ay'. Say it as 'TEL-er' with the r sound clearly present.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a job or a person without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: In American banks, the person who handles your deposits and withdrawals is called a teller, and you will see the word on signs and in banking apps. People say 'bank teller' for the job, and 'cashier' is more typical for stores and restaurants. A common request is 'Can I speak to a teller?' or 'I'd like to see a teller.'

distinctions.note: A cashier works at a register in a store or restaurant, while a teller handles money at a bank in the US.
A narrator tells a story in a book or film; 'teller' in the sense of storyteller is a less common usage.

examples.everyday: I just need to deposit this check, so I'll stop by the teller on my way out.
examples.professional: Our branch's teller staff handles most cash deposits, so the new software has to work at their stations.
examples.analytical: The teller's role has shrunk as automated machines and mobile banking have taken over routine transactions.

nuance.analogy: A teller is the human counter where money changes hands, like a clerk at a window who keeps the cash moving.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tellere, 'one who counts or relates,' from tellan, 'to count, reckon, relate.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'bank cashier' for a bank worker; Americans say 'bank teller' for a bank and 'cashier' for stores.
Pronouncing the last syllable as a full 'ur' vowel instead of a reduced rhotic schwa.

teller.etymology: From Middle English *tellere* (“one who counts or enumerates; one who recounts or relates; teller”), equivalent to *tell* + *-er*.

senses.definition: Frightening or intimidating.
senses.example: terrifying creature

senses.definition: Of a formidable nature; terrific.
senses.example: The new mathematician had a terrifying grasp of statistics that impressed everyone in the seminar.

core.definition: Extremely frightening or intimidating, causing great fear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Say the middle as 'rih' and the final '-ing' as a short, unstressed syllable, not 'eeng.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something causing intense fear, and it is also used jokingly for something very difficult ('a terrifying exam').
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'terrifying' for frightening events, experiences, or people, such as 'a terrifying ride.' In casual speech it is often used with some exaggeration, as when someone says a phone bill is terrifying. Be careful with the older sense 'terrific' (wonderful), which is not used in modern American English. A natural reply is 'That sounds terrifying! Are you okay?'

distinctions.note: 'Scary' is casual and common, often for movies or Halloween. 'Terrifying' is stronger and can describe real danger.
'Frightening' is neutral and widely used. 'Terrifying' suggests a more extreme level of fear.

examples.everyday: That roller coaster was terrifying, but I loved it.
examples.professional: The prospect of a production database failure is terrifying, so we test our backups every month.
examples.analytical: The problem of evil is terrifying to many believers because it seems to challenge God's goodness.

nuance.analogy: A terrifying thing is like a dark hallway with a sudden loud noise: it makes you freeze.
nuance.etymology: From terrify, from Latin terrificare, to frighten.
common_mistakes: Using 'terrifying' to mean 'wonderful' as in old-fashioned 'terrific.'
Saying 'I am terrifying' instead of 'I am terrified' when describing your own feeling.
patterns: it is terrifying to do sth

senses.definition: A software development process that relies on the repetition of a minimal development cycle where the developer writes an (initially failing) automated test case that defines a desired function, then produces minimal code to pass that test, and finally refactors the new code to acceptable standards.
senses.example: Our team adopted test-driven development, so every new function starts with a failing unit test.

core.definition: A programming practice where you write a failing automated test first, write the minimum code to pass it, then clean up the code.

pronunciation.tip: Stress test in the first word and VEL in development. Driven is weak and ends in a reduced -en sound. Developers usually say the abbreviation as the letters T-D-D.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional. Among developers it signals discipline and good engineering practice.
nuance.usage_note: Developers say test-driven development in full or just TDD, pronounced as the letters tee-dee-dee. It is a practice rather than a tool, so people say they practice TDD or work test-first. Writing tests after the code is common but is a different workflow. Asking do you do TDD? is a natural question in a technical interview or team discussion.

distinctions.note: Unit testing is the general practice of checking small pieces of code. TDD is a specific workflow in which the test is written before the code.
Behavior-driven development writes tests as plain-language scenarios about user behavior, while TDD tests focus on the units of code.

examples.everyday: My sister is a programmer, and she says her team does test-driven development at work.
examples.professional: We adopted test-driven development for the billing service, so every change starts with a failing test.
examples.analytical: Test-driven development treats the tests as a specification of behavior, so the design emerges from requirements rather than from the code.

nuance.analogy: Like writing the answer key before solving the puzzle, then solving only enough to match the key.
nuance.etymology: A compound of test, driven and development. The practice was popularized by Kent Beck around 2000.
common_mistakes: Thinking TDD just means having many tests. The defining feature is writing the test first and watching it fail.
Stressing driven as DRIV-en. The main stress belongs on TEST and VEL.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to text.
senses.example: I see that the editor revised the document's metadata, headers, and images, but I don't see any textual changes.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to textuality.
senses.example: The scholar's textual analysis revealed three competing versions of the Gospel of John.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to text as opposed to other document elements.
senses.example: I see that the editor revised the document's metadata, headers, and images, but I don't see any textual changes.

senses.definition: Pertaining to text messages, by analogy with sexual: textual harassment, textual intercourse; compare sexting.
senses.example: Their relationship turned toxic, with textual harassment flooding his phone every night.

core.definition: Relating to a written text, especially its exact wording, as in a book, document, manuscript or Scripture.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, TEKST. The tu sounds like 'ch' (as in 'virtual'), and the ending is reduced to 'uhl.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a property of a text without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use textual mostly in academic, legal, editorial and religious settings, as in 'textual evidence' in a classroom or 'textual errors' in a publication. In everyday talk people usually say 'the words' or 'what it actually says.' Do not confuse it with textural, which describes surface feel.
word_family: textualism (noun, a method of legal interpretation based on the written words)

distinctions.note: Textual relates to written words or documents, while textural relates to the feel or surface quality of something.
Textual refers to what is inside the text itself, while contextual refers to the surrounding circumstances in which it was written or read.

examples.everyday: My daughter's homework asks her to point to textual evidence for every claim she makes about the story.
examples.professional: Our editorial team flagged several textual inconsistencies between the draft and the final policy memo.
examples.analytical: A textual reading of the passage must attend to variant manuscripts before drawing any theological conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Textual analysis is like reading a recipe's exact wording line by line before judging the dish.
nuance.etymology: From Latin textus, 'woven, texture, text,' with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Confusing textual with textural, as in saying 'the textual of the bread' when you mean its texture.
Dropping the t in the tu sequence, so it sounds like TEKS-yoo-uhl instead of TEKST-choo-uhl.

textual.etymology: From Middle English *textewell*, *textueel*, *textuel*, *textuele*, *tixtuel* (“learned in texts, bookish”), possibly from Latin *textuālis*; also compare; or perhaps a coinage by Chaucer from Latin *textus* and Middle English *-el*.

related: textualism (noun, a method of legal interpretation based on the written words)

senses.definition: Saying the air conditioning is broken.

core.definition: A common sentence used to report that the air conditioning system is broken or not cooling the room.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters A and C separately as 'ay-see', with 'isn't' reduced quickly. The stress lands on WORK, and the r in working is American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical complaint or report.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when reporting a problem to a landlord, front desk, building manager or family member. In hot weather, people often say 'The AC is out' or 'The AC is broken' as well. Polite follow-ups include 'Could someone come take a look?' or 'When can someone check it?'

distinctions.note: More formal and complete; it suits written complaints or formal reports.

collocations: the AC is blowing warm air
call the landlord about the AC

examples.everyday: Hi, the AC isn't working in my apartment, and it's really hot in here.
examples.professional: Hi, I'm calling to report that the AC isn't working in Conference Room B, so the meeting may need to move.
examples.analytical: When the AC isn't working, the building's temperature control fails, which affects both comfort and equipment performance.

nuance.analogy: Like a fridge that stops humming: everything still exists, but the cooling is simply gone.
common_mistakes: Saying 'The AC is not work' without the -ing form.
Pronouncing 'AC' as a single word like 'ack' instead of 'ay-see'.

conversation.text: Hi, the AC isn't working, and it's ninety degrees in here.
The AC isn't working in the bedroom, so we slept in the living room.

core.definition: A clear sign of an approaching failure, defeat or unwelcome ending that people should recognize.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RY in writing and on WAWL, with ahn and thuh weak. Link the words so it sounds like 'thuh-RY-ting-ahn-thuh-WAWL'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It warns of trouble or the end of something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a situation clearly signals trouble, such as falling sales or repeated warnings from a manager. It is common in news and business talk, and it sounds dramatic, so use it carefully in formal settings. A natural reply is 'Yeah, we should have seen the writing on the wall.'

distinctions.note: A red flag is a warning sign that something needs attention. The writing on the wall suggests a definite, nearly inevitable outcome.
The handwriting on the wall is a variant with the same meaning. The writing on the wall is more common in American speech.

collocations: see the writing on the wall
the writing was on the wall
the writing on the wall for the company
read the writing on the wall

examples.everyday: When the factory closed its last shift, everyone in town could see the writing on the wall.
examples.professional: Three quarters of declining revenue is the writing on the wall, so we need a new plan before the board meets.
examples.analytical: Interpreting the writing on the wall requires separating visible signs from the deeper structural causes that produce them.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather radar that shows a storm coming before the first drop of rain.
nuance.etymology: From the biblical account in Daniel 5, in which writing appears on a wall at Belshazzar's feast.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the writing in the wall'; the preposition is on.
Using it for a neutral message; it signals a warning about a bad outcome.
nuance.biblical_note: In Daniel 5, King Belshazzar of Babylon holds a feast and sees a hand writing on the plaster of the palace wall. No one can read the writing until Daniel is brought in to interpret it. The Aramaic words are mene, mene, tekel and peres, which Daniel explains as a judgment that the king's reign is numbered, weighed and divided. Daniel 5:5 describes the appearance of the fingers writing. Daniel 5:25-28 gives Daniel's interpretation of the words. Belshazzar is killed that same night, according to Daniel 5:30.

senses.definition: Of, from, or pertaining to, Thessaloniki.
Someone or something from, or pertaining to, Thessaloniki.
senses.example: The apostle Paul's letter to the Thessalonian church addresses persecution and the return of Christ.

core.definition: Of or from Thessaloniki, the Greek port city; as a noun, a person who is from Thessaloniki or lived there in antiquity.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOH, and the last syllable is a weak 'un' rather than a full 'ee-an.' The th is voiceless, as in 'think,' not the voiced 'th' of 'this'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise descriptive term for people and places, with a religious sense in the New Testament context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Thessalonian mainly in historical, religious, or academic writing, especially when discussing Paul's letters to the church in Thessalonica. For everyday talk about someone from the city, people more often say 'someone from Thessaloniki' or 'a Greek from Thessaloniki.'

distinctions.note: Thessaloniki is the modern city's name, while Thessalonian is the adjective or noun for its people and things.
Thessalian refers to Thessaly, a different region of Greece, not to the city of Thessaloniki.

examples.everyday: My cousin married a Thessalonian, so we visit Greece almost every summer.
examples.professional: The company's Thessalonian branch handles all of our shipping in the Balkans.
examples.analytical: Paul's Thessalonian letters are among the earliest New Testament writings, addressed to a young church facing persecution.

nuance.analogy: Thessalonian is to Thessaloniki what Parisian is to Paris.
nuance.etymology: From Thessalonica, the ancient city named for Thessalonike, half-sister of Alexander the Great.
common_mistakes: Confusing Thessalonian with Thessalian, which refers to Thessaly.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ee-an' instead of a weak 'un.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word Thessalonikeis (Θεσσαλονικεῖς) means the people of Thessalonica, and the New Testament letters are addressed to them. Acts 17:1-9 describes Paul's visit to Thessalonica and the disturbance that followed his preaching there. First Thessalonians 4:13-18 addresses believers' questions about those who have died and the coming of the Lord, offering comfort to the grieving church. Second Thessalonians 3:6-13 deals with idleness among some members and urges them to work for their living.

senses.definition: A thing as it is independent of any conceptualization or perception by the human mind, postulated by practical reason but existing in a condition which is in principle unknowable and unexperienceable.
senses.example: Kant insisted that the thing-in-itself lies beyond anything we can ever experience.

core.definition: In Kant's philosophy, a thing as it is in itself, independent of how the human mind perceives or conceptualizes it, and therefore unknowable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on "self," the last syllable of the final word, while "thing" and "in" carry lighter secondary stress. Say "it" quickly and reduce it to "ut" in fast speech. The "ng" in "thing" is one sound, not "ng" plus "g."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in philosophy and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "thing-in-itself" mainly in philosophy courses, academic writing, and discussions of Kant. It usually appears in its German form, "Ding an sich," in scholarly texts. In everyday speech it would sound odd, so people use "reality" or "the thing as it really is."

distinctions.note: A phenomenon is a thing as it appears to us, while the thing-in-itself is the thing as it is independent of appearance.
Noumenon is a closely related Kantian term for an object of pure understanding; for Kant, the thing-in-itself is the unknowable reality behind appearances.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor said Kant believed we never know things exactly as they really are, which he called the thing-in-itself.
examples.professional: The essay argues that the thing-in-itself is useful as a limit concept even if it is not directly knowable.
examples.analytical: Kant's postulation of the thing-in-itself grounds his claim that appearances are structured by the mind without being created by it.

nuance.analogy: The thing-in-itself is like the actual fruit inside a sealed jar: you see its shape through the glass, but you never touch it directly.
nuance.etymology: A translation of German Ding an sich, the term used by Immanuel Kant in the 1780s.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphens and writing "thing in itself" in formal writing.
Confusing the thing-in-itself with the phenomenon, which is what appears to us.
Stressing "thing" as the main beat instead of "self."

senses.definition: A unique, concrete and irreducible essence or identity of a particular thing or individual, distinguishing it from others of the same kind.

core.definition: The unique, concrete identity of a particular individual thing, what makes it this one and not another of its kind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the final -ness reduced to a short schwa. Use the voiced th of 'this' and don't add an extra vowel between s and n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise philosophical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thisness almost only in philosophy and theology courses or texts, especially when discussing medieval thinkers such as Duns Scotus. In everyday talk it would sound odd or pretentious. Philosophers in the US often prefer the Latin-derived term haecceity when they want a more technical word.

distinctions.note: Quiddity names what a thing is, its essence or whatness, while thisness names what makes it this particular thing.
Haecceity is the more technical Latin-based term, and thisness is the English rendering used in many translations and courses.

examples.everyday: My philosophy friend kept talking about thisness, but I had no idea what he meant.
examples.professional: In the seminar, the presenter explained how thisness distinguishes individual substances in medieval metaphysics.
examples.analytical: Scotus argued that thisness is not an additional ingredient added to a common nature, but the nature's own individuation.

nuance.analogy: Like a fingerprint: many people share a common kind, but each one has a unique identity that no other has.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from 'this' plus the suffix '-ness', as a rendering of Latin haecceitas.
common_mistakes: Using thisness as if it means ordinary 'this one' in casual conversation.
Confusing it with quiddity, which refers to essence rather than individual identity.

senses.definition: Demonstrating thought or careful consideration.
senses.example: Most thoughtful people eventually solve the puzzle.

senses.definition: Demonstrating kindness or consideration for others.
senses.example: Preparing dinner is a thoughtful gesture for a new mother.

core.definition: Showing careful thought, or showing kindness and consideration for other people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ful is a reduced syllable pronounced 'fuhl', not 'fool'. Many Americans with the cot-caught merger say this with an 'ah' vowel, which is also acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; praising someone's care or consideration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'That's thoughtful of you' when someone gives a gift or does a kind favor. It can also describe a careful, reflective answer or essay. It is friendly and polite in everyday speech and common at work.

distinctions.note: Considerate focuses on avoiding harm or inconvenience to others, while thoughtful can also describe careful reflection.
Pensive describes a quiet, dreamy or sad mood, while thoughtful describes deliberate consideration.

examples.everyday: Thanks for bringing soup when I was sick, that was really thoughtful of you.
examples.professional: Thanks for the thoughtful feedback on the proposal, it helped us tighten the timeline.
examples.analytical: A thoughtful reading of the argument considers both its premises and the objections it anticipates.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned instrument: each note is chosen with care so the whole piece sounds right.
nuance.etymology: From thought plus the suffix -ful, meaning full of thought.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'thought-FULL'.
Using thoughtful to mean thinking in general without the sense of care or consideration.
patterns: it is thoughtful of sb to do sth

senses.definition: The characteristic of using a minimum of something (especially money).
senses.example: His thrift can be seen in how little the trashman takes from his house.

senses.definition: A savings bank.
senses.example: Usually, home mortgages are obtained from thrifts.

senses.definition: Any of various plants of the genus Armeria, particularly Armeria maritima.
senses.example: Pink thrift bloomed along the rocky cliffs near the coastal trail.

senses.definition: To shop or browse at a thrift shop; to buy (something) at a thrift shop.
senses.example: They like to go thrifting on weekends.

core.definition: The habit of using money and resources carefully and avoiding waste; economical management.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin', and the vowel is short, as in 'sit'. Keep the final 'ft' as a clean consonant cluster, with no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive; thrift suggests responsible, admirable care with money, though it can slip toward stinginess when overdone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thrift to praise careful spending, especially in personal finance, family life, and shopping. In everyday talk, people more often say 'being frugal' or 'saving money', and thrift sounds slightly formal or traditional. The word also names a plant, Armeria maritima, but that sense is rare in daily speech.

distinctions.note: Frugality is a more deliberate and disciplined form of saving, while thrift is more about wise management of resources.
Economy can mean an economic system or efficiency, while thrift is personal care with money or resources.
Stinginess is negative and suggests refusing to spend even when it is reasonable; thrift is positive.

examples.everyday: My mom taught us the value of thrift, so we always fixed things instead of throwing them away.
examples.professional: Our procurement policy encourages thrift by requiring two quotes before any purchase over five hundred dollars.
examples.analytical: Early American writers often praised thrift as a Christian virtue, linking careful stewardship of money with moral discipline.

nuance.analogy: Thrift is like a gardener who uses every bit of rain and compost, so nothing goes to waste and the whole garden grows.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse þrift 'prosperity, success', from þrífa 'to grasp, thrive'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'th' as a voiced sound, as in 'this'.
Using thrift as an adjective; the adjective is thrifty.

thrift.etymology: From Middle English *thrift*, *thryfte*, *þrift*, from Old Norse *þrift* (“thriving condition, prosperity”).

senses.definition: An attack made by moving the sword parallel to its length and landing with the point.
senses.example: Pierre was a master swordsman, and could parry the thrusts of lesser men with barely a thought.

senses.definition: A push, stab, or lunge forward.
senses.example: The cutpurse tried to knock her satchel from her hands, but she avoided his thrust and yelled, "Thief!"

senses.definition: The force generated by propulsion, as in a jet engine.
senses.example: Spacecraft are engineering marvels, designed to resist the thrust of liftoff, as well as the reverse pressure of the void.

senses.definition: The primary effort; the goal.
senses.example: Ostensibly, the class was about public health in general, but the main thrust was really sex education.

senses.definition: To make advance with force.
senses.example: We thrust at the enemy with our forces.

senses.definition: To force something upon someone.
senses.example: I asked her not to thrust the responsibility on me.

senses.definition: To push out or extend rapidly or powerfully.
senses.example: He thrust his arm into the icy stream and grabbed a wriggling fish, astounding the observers.

senses.definition: To push or drive with force; to shove.
senses.example: to thrust anything with the hand or foot, or with an instrument

senses.definition: To enter by pushing; to squeeze in.
senses.example: He thrust his way through the crowded train and grabbed a seat.

senses.definition: To stab; to pierce; usually with through.
senses.example: The knight thrust his sword through the dragon's scales.

core.definition: A strong, forceful push or lunge forward; also, the forward force an engine or jet produces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, and the th is voiceless as in 'think.' Keep the vowel short, like the u in 'cut', and do not add an extra vowel before the final st.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be aggressive when describing a physical attack, and neutral when describing engines or politics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thrust in everyday speech for a forceful push, and in technical speech for engine power, such as 'jet thrust.' In business and politics it means the main point or direction of an argument, as in 'the thrust of the proposal.' Phrases like 'the main thrust of' are natural in meetings and news.

distinctions.note: Push is the everyday word, while thrust suggests more force, sharpness or suddenness.
A lunge is a sudden movement of the body toward something, while a thrust can be a deliberate push or stab.

examples.everyday: He gave the broken gate a thrust with his shoulder and it finally opened.
examples.professional: The main thrust of my proposal is to cut the data pipeline's latency by half.
examples.analytical: The author's central thrust is that moral authority depends on humility rather than power.

nuance.analogy: Like a rocket engine that pushes everything forward, a thrust is a steady or sudden force driving motion in one direction.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English thrusten, from Old Norse þrýsta, to press or squeeze.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel, saying 'thr-us-ta' or 'THRUST-uh.'
Using thrust as a verb in the noun sense, as in 'the thrust of the policy' is fine but 'I thrust the idea' is less natural than 'I pushed the idea.'

thrust.etymology: From Middle English *þristen*, from Old Norse *þrysta*, from Proto-Germanic **þrustijaną*, possibly from Proto-Indo-European **trewd-*.

senses.definition: A regularly-shaped slab of clay or other material, affixed to cover or decorate a surface, as in a roof-tile, glazed tile, stove tile, carpet tile, etc.
senses.example: We replaced the cracked bathroom tile with a glazed ceramic tile in soft blue.

senses.definition: A rectangular graphic.
senses.example: Each tile within the map consists of 256 × 256 pixels.

senses.definition: Any of various flat cuboid playing pieces used in certain games, such as dominoes, Scrabble, or mahjong.
senses.example: Each player drew seven tiles from the pile before the mahjong game began.

senses.definition: (Lego building) A Lego piece that is 1/3 the height of a brick, and is smooth without studs on top.
senses.example: The model needed a smooth one-by-two tile to finish the flat roof of the spaceship.

senses.definition: (dated) A stiff hat.
senses.example: He tipped his tile to the ladies as he passed them on Fifth Avenue.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To cover with tiles.
senses.example: The handyman tiled the kitchen.

senses.definition: To arrange in a regular pattern, with adjoining edges (applied to tile-like objects, graphics, windows in a computer interface).
senses.example: In the design app, you can tile the background image across the whole canvas.

senses.definition: To optimize (a loop in program code) by means of the tiling technique.
senses.example: The compiler can tile the nested loop to keep the data in the processor cache.

senses.definition: To seal a lodge against intrusions from unauthorized people.
senses.example: The Masonic officers gathered at dusk to tile the lodge before the ceremony began.

senses.definition: To protect from the intrusion of the uninitiated.
senses.example: to tile a Masonic lodge

core.definition: A thin, flat piece of ceramic, stone, or similar material used to cover floors, walls, or roofs.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables; the second is a syllabic l that sounds like 'uhl' with no separate vowel. Don't say 'tie-ELL'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, everyday word in home and building talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tile' for floors, bathrooms, and kitchen backsplashes; 'ceramic tile' is a common phrase. A hardware store clerk might ask, 'What kind of tile are you looking for?' For roofs, Americans often say 'shingles' for asphalt and 'roof tiles' for clay or concrete tiles.

distinctions.note: A brick is a solid block of fired clay used in walls, while a tile is a thin slab used as a surface covering.
Carpet is a soft textile floor covering, while tile is hard, flat, and easy to clean.

examples.everyday: We're going to put new tile in the kitchen this summer.
examples.professional: The contractor priced the bathroom job by the square foot of tile.
examples.analytical: The mosaic's meaning depends on how each tile contributes to a larger pattern, which the viewer perceives only from a distance.

nuance.analogy: Like a single square in a checkerboard that completes the whole board.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'tegula', meaning roof tile, from 'tegere', to cover.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'tile' with a long e as 'TEEL'; it rhymes with 'mile'.
Using 'tile' for an asphalt roof; Americans usually say 'shingles' for that.

tile.etymology: From Middle English *tile,tyl,tigel,tiȝel,teȝele*, from Old English *tiġele,tieġle,tiġle* (“tile, brick”), from **tigulā* (“tile, brick”), from Proto-Germanic **tigulǭ* (“tile, brick”), from Latin *tēgula*, from Proto-Indo-European **teg-* (“to cover”).

senses.definition: The amount of time an algorithm requires to run, as a function of the amount of input, measured in such a way as to ignore constant terms and multiplication by constant terms.
senses.example: Sorting with merge sort has a time complexity of n log n in the average case.

core.definition: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as its input grows, written in Big O notation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TIME first, then PLEK in complexity, and the -ity ending is a reduced vowel. Many learners stress the -plex syllable incorrectly or pronounce the final syllable as 'tee' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers and computer science students use this term constantly in interviews and code reviews. Say 'the time complexity is linear' or 'this is O of n squared' in conversation. Often it is paired with space complexity.

distinctions.note: Time complexity measures how running time grows with input size, while space complexity measures how much memory the algorithm needs.

examples.everyday: My nephew is studying for coding interviews and keeps asking me what time complexity means.
examples.professional: Before we merge this change, can you check the time complexity of the sorting step? It may slow down large batches.
examples.analytical: The proof establishes an upper bound on time complexity, though it says nothing about the constant factors that dominate in practice.

nuance.analogy: Time complexity is like a commute estimate: it describes how the travel time grows as you add more stops, not the exact minutes on a given day.
nuance.etymology: Compound of time (Old English tima) and complexity (from Latin complexus, interwoven).
common_mistakes: Confusing time complexity with actual running time in seconds, which depends on hardware.
Stressing complexity on the wrong syllable, as in 'kum-PLEX-i-tee' with the wrong vowel.

senses.definition: That tingles.
senses.example: tingling sensation in one's wrists

senses.definition: A tingling sensation; pins and needles.
senses.example: A tingling ran up my arm after I sat on my foot too long.

core.definition: Causing a light prickling or buzzing feeling on the skin, often from cold, excitement or a numb limb.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The g is hard, and the middle syllable is a weak uh sound, so do not say 'ting-GULL-ing' with a loud vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing excitement or freshness; it can be a worrying sign when describing a persistent symptom.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'my fingers are tingling' or 'a tingling feeling' for a prickly sensation, often from cold or a limb that fell asleep. If tingling in the hands or feet keeps happening, mention it to a doctor. The everyday phrase for the same feeling is pins and needles.

distinctions.note: Prickly suggests a sharp stinging on the skin or a touchy person; tingling is a lighter, buzzing sensation.
Numb means having no feeling; tingling is an active sensation that often comes before or after numbness.
Thrilling describes excitement in general; tingling can describe a physical feeling of excitement.

examples.everyday: My feet are tingling after sitting on the floor for so long.
examples.professional: The nurse asked whether the tingling in his hands had started after the procedure.
examples.analytical: The tingling of anticipation in the opening chapter is less a physical sensation than a moral warning.

nuance.analogy: Tingling is like static on a radio: a faint buzzing that shows a signal is there but not yet clear.
nuance.etymology: From the verb tingle, from Middle English tinglen, a frequentative of tingen, to ring or tinkle.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g as a soft j sound
Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'ting-GLING'

senses.definition: A particle used for marking the following verb as an infinitive.
senses.example: I want to leave.

senses.definition: As above, with the verb implied.
senses.example: "Did you visit the museum?" "I wanted to, but it was closed."

senses.definition: Used to indicate an obligation on the part of, or a directive given to, the subject.
senses.example: You are to go to the store and buy a bottle of milk.

senses.definition: A filler word common amongst urban Indians.
senses.example: I am to so bored right now.

senses.definition: In order to.
senses.example: I went to the shops to buy some bread.

senses.definition: In the direction of; towards.
senses.example: She looked to the heavens.

senses.definition: Indicating destination or final position: In the direction of, so as to arrive at or reach.
senses.example: We are walking to the shop.

senses.definition: Used to indicate the target or recipient of an action.
senses.example: I gave the book to him.

senses.definition: So as to contact, press against, impact, etc.
senses.example: I fixed the notice to the wall.

senses.definition: So as to become or reach: indicating a terminal state resulting from an action.
senses.example: His face was beaten to a pulp.

senses.definition: So as to bring about or elicit (an effect or outcome).
senses.example: He made several bad-taste jokes to groans from the audience.

senses.definition: Used after an adjective to indicate its application.
senses.example: similar to ..., relevant to ..., pertinent to ..., I was nice to him, he was cruel to her, I am used to walking.

senses.definition: Indicating a degree or level reached.
senses.example: It was to a large extent true.

senses.definition: Used to describe what something consists of or contains.
senses.example: Anyone could do this job; there's nothing to it.

senses.definition: Denotes the end of a range.
senses.example: It takes 2 to 4 weeks to process typical applications.

senses.definition: Used to indicate a ratio or comparison; compared to, as against.
senses.example: one to one = 1:1

senses.definition: Used to indicate that the preceding term is to be raised to the power of the following value; indicates exponentiation.
senses.example: Three squared or three to the second power is nine.

senses.definition: Preceding (the stated hour).
senses.example: What's the time? – It's quarter to four in the afternoon (or 3:45 pm).

senses.definition: With implied hour.
senses.example: It’s quarter to.

senses.definition: According to.
senses.example: Our holiday did not go to plan.

senses.definition: Used more-or-less idiomatically with various verbs: keep to the left, agree to the proposal, attend to the matter, etc. See the individual entries.
senses.example: Please attend to the matter of the missing invoice before the audit next week.

senses.definition: Toward a closed, touching, or engaging position.
senses.example: Please push the door to.

senses.definition: Into the wind.
senses.example: The sailors brought the boat to, holding her head into the wind.

core.definition: Indicating movement toward a place, person, or goal, or the end point of an action.

pronunciation.tip: In most sentences 'to' is a reduced 'tuh,' as in 'going to the store.' Say the full 'TOO' only when it is stressed, as at the end of a phrase, for example 'pull the door to.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is one of the most common words in English and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: 'To' is among the most frequent words in American English, and it appears in countless everyday phrases such as 'go to work' and 'listen to music.' Americans usually reduce it to 'tuh' in speech, so learners should practice the reduced form. Be careful with 'to' versus 'too' and 'two' in writing, since they sound the same in many contexts.

distinctions.note: 'Too' means 'also' or 'excessively,' while 'to' is a preposition or infinitive marker; they are often confused in writing.
'Toward' and 'to' both show direction, but 'toward' emphasizes movement in a general direction rather than a specific end point.

examples.everyday: I'm going to the store after lunch.
examples.professional: I'll send the revised budget to the team by Friday.
examples.analytical: Kant's argument turns to the question of whether reason alone can ground morality.

nuance.analogy: 'To' is like an arrow on a map: it points from where you are to where you are going.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tō, 'toward' or 'to.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'to,' 'too,' and 'two' in writing.
Saying 'I want that you come' instead of 'I want you to come.'

to.etymology: From Middle English *to*, from Old English *tō*, from Proto-Germanic **tō* ~ **ta*, from Proto-Indo-European **de* ~ **do* (“to”).

senses.definition: To abide by the rules or conventions; to follow the party line.
senses.example: Television shows these days do not always toe the line of decency and common sense.

senses.definition: To stand at one's mark before a footrace.
senses.example: Alberto Salazar is one of the most famous athletes to have toed the line at this great race.

senses.definition: To be on a boundary or in a gray area between two states.
senses.example: Her stories often toe the line between fact and fiction.

core.definition: To obey rules or conform to what a group expects, especially when pressure is applied to do so.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LINE, and 'the' is reduced to 'thuh' before a consonant. In fast speech, 'toe the' links together, so it sounds like toh-thuh-LINE, not three separate words with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests conforming, and it can imply reluctant obedience to pressure from a leader or group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in workplaces, sports, politics and families, usually when someone must follow a rule or leader they may not fully like, as in 'Everyone has to toe the line on the new policy.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'll toe the line,' or a simple agreement. It is idiomatic, so do not use it for literal lines on the ground except in the origin context of footraces.

distinctions.note: 'Fall in line' emphasizes joining a group or following orders, while 'toe the line' emphasizes strict compliance with rules.
'Go along with' can be a passive agreement, while 'toe the line' implies following rules even when there is pressure.

collocations: toe the line on the budget

examples.everyday: My dad told us we had to toe the line on bedtime, or we would lose screen time.
examples.professional: New hires are expected to toe the line on security training, or they won't get system access.
examples.analytical: Scholars who challenge orthodoxy often find that institutions expect them to toe the line in exchange for tenure.

nuance.analogy: Like runners waiting behind the starting line, you stay where the group expects you to be.
nuance.etymology: From footraces, where competitors stood with their toes right at the starting line.
common_mistakes: Saying 'toe on the line' or 'step the line,' which are not standard forms.
Taking it literally, when it is an idiom meaning to conform to rules or expectations.

toe-the-line.etymology: with multiple competing etymologies and some theorizing the phrasing originated from the United States and others the United Kingdom.

senses.definition: Of or relating to topology.
Equipped with a topology that is typically required to be compatible with the underlying structure in some way.
senses.example: topological group

core.definition: Relating to topology, the branch of mathematics that studies properties of shapes that stay the same when the shape is stretched or bent without tearing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LAH, the third syllable. Many learners put the stress on 'top'; keep the 'o' in the middle reduced, and say the final syllable as a light 'kuhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and data scientists use topological to describe properties or spaces studied in topology. Outside math, Americans might use it loosely, as in 'a topological view of networks,' but the word is strongly tied to its technical meaning. In casual conversation it may sound too specialized.

distinctions.note: Topographical refers to the surface features of land on a map, while topological refers to abstract properties of shapes or spaces that survive continuous deformation.
