core.definition: Impossible to measure, or so large or small that it cannot be measured accurately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MEH. The 'zh' sound is like the 's' in 'measure', and the final -able is a reduced 'uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It often describes something vast or valuable beyond calculation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually use immeasurable or 'impossible to measure' in everyday talk. Unmeasurable is more common in technical and literary writing, especially in statistics or philosophy. It is not a strong daily word, but it is correct.

distinctions.note: Immeasurable is more common in everyday and literary English and emphasizes vastness. Unmeasurable is more neutral and technical.
Unmeasured means it has not been measured yet, but it could be. Unmeasurable means it cannot be measured at all.

examples.everyday: The sunset over the lake had an unmeasurable beauty that no photo could capture.
examples.professional: Some of the project's benefits, like team trust, are unmeasurable with our current metrics.
examples.analytical: Theologians have argued that God's grace is unmeasurable by any human standard of merit.

nuance.analogy: An unmeasurable quantity is like the depth of the ocean from a small rowboat: you know it is there, but no ruler can reach its bottom.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus measurable, from measure, from Latin mensura.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'mesh-ur' with no 'zh' sound.
Using it when the thing is merely unknown; unmeasurable means it cannot be measured in principle.

senses.definition: Not perturbed.
senses.example: Despite the shouting in the lobby, the old clerk remained unperturbed and kept stamping forms.

core.definition: Calm and not worried, upset, or disturbed, even when something difficult or surprising happens.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TURBD, the main syllable, and it is a single syllable ending in a 'b' followed by 'd', so do not add an extra 'ed' syllable. The first syllables are light and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes composure and steadiness under pressure, which Americans usually admire, especially in leaders, professionals, and people in crisis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in news reports, reviews, workplace praise, and descriptions of people who stay calm, as in 'She remained unperturbed.' In casual talk, 'totally chill' or 'didn't even blink' is more common. It is often paired with 'by' to name the cause of the calm, as in 'unperturbed by the criticism.'

distinctions.note: Composed describes outward calm and self-control; unperturbed describes being untouched by the disturbance in the first place.
Indifferent means not caring at all, which can be negative; unperturbed means calm under pressure, which is usually positive.

examples.everyday: The waiter dropped a whole tray of drinks, but he stayed totally unperturbed and just grabbed a mop.
examples.professional: Even after the server outage, the on-call engineer stayed unperturbed and walked the team through the rollback.
examples.analytical: The Stoic sage remains unperturbed by external events, since he holds that only his own judgments are truly within his control.

nuance.analogy: Like a deep lake that stays still when a pebble hits the surface, an unperturbed person absorbs the disturbance without rippling.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus perturbed, from Latin perturbare, 'to disturb thoroughly', from per- (thoroughly) plus turbare (to disturb).
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable and saying 'un-per-TURB-ed', which sounds unnatural; the ending is one syllable.
Stressing the per- syllable instead of TURBD, which blurs the word.

senses.definition: Not problematic (presenting problems) or not controversial.

core.definition: Not causing difficulties or problems; easy to handle, or not controversial.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MAT, the syllable before -ic. The first 'prob' uses the American 'ah' vowel, the same vowel as in 'cot', and the middle syllables are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it signals that something will work smoothly and needs no special attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in the workplace and in academic writing: 'The update should be unproblematic.' It can sound stiff in casual talk, where 'no problem' or 'easy' is more common. It is applied to plans, tasks and ideas, not usually to people.

distinctions.note: Easy describes how hard something is to do; unproblematic describes the absence of issues or complications in a plan or result.
Uncontroversial means no one disagrees; unproblematic can mean there are no practical problems, even if people disagree about other matters.

examples.everyday: Moving the appointment to Friday should be unproblematic, so just text the clinic.
examples.professional: The migration is unproblematic for most users, but two legacy reports will need manual updates.
examples.analytical: Historians once treated the Enlightenment as an unproblematic story of progress, but recent scholarship complicates that account.

nuance.analogy: Like a road with no potholes, where the drive goes smoothly from start to finish.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus problematic, from Greek problēma 'something put forward, an obstacle'.
common_mistakes: Using it for a person, as in 'he is unproblematic'; it sounds odd for people, so use 'easy to work with' instead.
Stressing 'PROB' instead of 'MAT', which moves the stress away from the American pattern.

senses.definition: Unbecoming of a professional; hence inappropriate in the workplace.
senses.example: unprofessional behavior

senses.definition: Lacking a profession.
Not relating to professional occupation or employment; nonprofessional.
senses.example: The festival welcomed unprofessional bands, students, and hobbyists alongside the paid musicians.

senses.definition: One who is not a professional.
senses.example: The hackathon was open to unprofessionals, but the judges were all industry engineers.

core.definition: Not conforming to the standards of behavior expected in a workplace or professional field; inappropriate for someone doing professional work.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FESH, with a lighter secondary stress on un-. The -ional ending is pronounced /ənəl/, and the middle syllables reduce to a quick uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone unprofessional is a serious criticism at work and can affect reputation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for rude emails, showing up late, gossiping in meetings, or sending messages at inappropriate times. Saying it directly to a coworker is usually a strong statement, so people often say 'that wasn't the best look' or 'maybe keep it more formal' instead. The noun sense, meaning one who is not a professional, is rare and mainly seen in older or technical writing.

distinctions.note: Nonprofessional means not belonging to a profession, such as a volunteer or amateur; unprofessional means behaving poorly for a professional role, which is an insult.
Rude is about manners toward people; unprofessional is about workplace conduct, including punctuality, communication, and judgment.
Unethical describes a violation of moral or legal principles; unprofessional is a lighter charge about failing to meet workplace standards.

examples.everyday: Honestly, texting your boss at midnight to complain about the schedule sounded a little unprofessional.
examples.professional: Replying all to the client's complaint with sarcastic jokes was unprofessional, so please use the approved template next time.
examples.analytical: A code of conduct defines what counts as unprofessional, but the boundary between candor and disrespect remains contested.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who starts arguing with the players: one lapse in conduct can undermine trust in the whole game.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus professional, from Latin professio, 'public declaration,' via professional's sense of a vocation one openly commits to.
common_mistakes: Using 'unprofessional' to mean 'nonprofessional' or 'amateur' for a volunteer; it implies bad conduct, so it can offend.
Stressing the wrong syllable: say un-pruh-FESH-uh-nul, not un-PRO-fession-al.

senses.definition: Not restricted or confined.
Having no security classification.
senses.example: The report was marked unrestricted, so anyone in the department could read it.

core.definition: Not limited, controlled, or confined by rules, conditions, or boundaries; open for anyone to use or enter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRIK, the second main syllable, with un- lightly stressed. Reduce the re to a short rih sound, and pronounce the -ted ending as tid, with a clear vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing freedom or access; negative when describing unchecked power or authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it often in travel, technology, and business, as in unrestricted access, unrestricted Wi-Fi, or an unrestricted visa. In everyday talk they usually say no limits or open access. It sounds formal but is very common on signs and in policies.

distinctions.note: Unlimited refers to quantity or amount with no cap, while unrestricted refers to access, freedom, or permission with no confining rules.
Unconditional means with no conditions attached to a promise or offer, while unrestricted means with no limits on use or access.

examples.everyday: The hotel gives you unrestricted access to the pool and the gym, so you can go whenever you like.
examples.professional: Give the new analyst unrestricted read access to the warehouse data, but keep write permissions limited to the data team.
examples.analytical: Mill argued that liberty is endangered when state power is unrestricted, because no principle limits its reach.

nuance.analogy: Like an open highway with no gates, tolls, or closed lanes.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + restricted, from Latin restringere 'to bind back'.
common_mistakes: Using unrestricted for unlimited when a large but finite amount is meant
Pronouncing the re- as ree instead of the reduced rih

senses.definition: Not utterable; incapable of being physically spoken or voiced; unpronounceable.
senses.example: Some Hebrew names were considered unutterable, so readers substituted other words.

senses.definition: Incapable of being articulated or expressed; indescribable, inexpressible.
senses.example: unutterable anguish

senses.definition: Not allowed to be spoken; taboo, unspeakable.
senses.example: In that household, the topic of her brother's crime was unutterable at the dinner table.

senses.definition: Extremely bad or objectionable; unspeakable.
senses.example: The conditions in the prison were unutterable, and the reporter struggled to describe them.

senses.definition: Something which is unutterable (incapable of being physically spoken, incapable of being articulated or expressed, etc.).
senses.example: She tried to explain her grief, but it remained an unutterable that no words could reach.

core.definition: Too extreme, intense or terrible to be put into words; impossible to describe adequately.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the second syllable, UT, not on un-. The tt in utter is a flap in American speech, so it sounds close to 'UH-der', and the ending is a weak 'uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly emotional and usually dramatic. It intensifies a feeling, most often a negative one (unutterable sorrow) but sometimes a positive one (unutterable joy).
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing, speeches, eulogies and poetry to say that something is beyond words. In everyday conversation people say 'indescribable' or 'I can't even describe it' instead. Using it casually can sound overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Indescribable is the everyday word for something too good or bad to put into words, while unutterable is more formal and carries a sense of deep emotion or solemnity.
Unspeakable can mean outrageously bad or too shameful to name, while unutterable leans toward strong feeling or the sacred and is less tied to moral outrage.

examples.everyday: When the doctor called to say the surgery went well, my dad's relief was unutterable.
examples.professional: After the outage ended, the relief in the room was almost unutterable, though nobody could quite put it into words in the retrospective.
examples.analytical: For Augustine, God is so far beyond human language that the divine essence is in a sense unutterable, so our speech about God is always an approximation.

nuance.analogy: Like the taste of a wine you know well but cannot name; the experience is clear, yet no word fits it.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus utterable, from utter, from Middle English uttren 'to put out, speak', from out.
common_mistakes: Using it for everyday annoyances, as in 'the traffic was unutterable', which sounds overdramatic.
Stressing the first syllable, saying UN-utter-able, instead of un-UT-er-uh-buhl.
nuance.biblical_note: In 2 Corinthians 12:4 Paul describes being caught up into Paradise and hearing words that cannot be told; the Greek phrase arrhēta rhēmata means things not to be spoken. In Romans 8:26 Paul says the Spirit intercedes with groanings too deep for words, using the Greek adjective alalētos, not capable of being spoken. In 1 Peter 1:8 the joy of believers in Christ is described as inexpressible, using the Greek anekdiēgētos, not capable of being fully told.

senses.definition: The property of being unwilling.
senses.example: His unwillingness to admit a mistake frustrated everyone on the project team.

core.definition: The state of not wanting to do something, or of being reluctant to act or agree.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on WIL. The final syllable 'ness' is short and reduced, and the 'ing' is pronounced with a clear 'ing' sound rather than 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a reasonable hesitation or an obstinate refusal, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in formal or professional settings, such as explaining why a deal stalled or why someone is resisting a change. In casual speech they more often say 'they didn't want to' or 'they weren't into it.' It works well in news reporting and in workplace discussions.

distinctions.note: Reluctance is a feeling of hesitation; unwillingness is a broader stance of not wanting to act at all.
Refusal is an explicit statement of 'no'; unwillingness can be a quiet state that never gets stated.

examples.everyday: Her unwillingness to talk about the accident made us worry even more.
examples.professional: The team's unwillingness to adopt the new tool is slowing down the migration.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats the human unwillingness to love God as a deeper problem than mere ignorance of the truth.

nuance.analogy: Unwillingness is like a locked door with no handle on the inside: the person is there, but nothing is going to open it.
nuance.etymology: From 'unwilling' (not willing), plus the suffix '-ness,' which turns an adjective into a noun.
common_mistakes: Saying 'unwillingless' or misspelling the double 'l' in 'unwilling' as one 'l'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ness' with a long e sound.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a usufruct.
senses.example: The usufructuary rights to the orchard passed to his widow, though she could not sell the land.

senses.definition: A person who holds property, or the use of assets, by usufruct; a fructuary.
senses.example: As a usufructuary, the tenant could harvest the timber but never cut down the forest.

core.definition: Relating to a legal right to use and enjoy another person's property without owning it or damaging its substance.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FRUCT, where the vowel is the 'uh' of 'cut,' not the 'oo' of 'food.' The 'j' in the first syllable is optional, and the final '-ary' is reduced to 'ur-ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a legal term with no emotional force.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'usufructuary' mainly in law, estate planning, property, and academic writing about civil law systems. In everyday talk, people say 'the right to use the property' or 'life estate' instead. A trust or will may name a usufructuary, meaning someone who receives income or use while someone else keeps the title.

distinctions.note: A tenant leases property under a rental agreement and pays rent, while a usufructuary holds a right to enjoy property and must preserve it.
An owner holds full title and can sell or change the property, while a usufructuary holds only the right to use it and take its benefits.
A lessee holds rights under a contract for a fixed term, while a usufruct usually arises from ownership, will, or law and is not a rental.

examples.everyday: My lawyer said my aunt is only a usufructuary, which means she can live in the house but can't sell it.
examples.professional: The trust names the spouse as usufructuary, so the children keep title while she receives the income from the land.
examples.analytical: The usufructuary is bound to preserve the substance of the property, and that duty distinguishes the right from full ownership.

nuance.analogy: Like borrowing a friend's car for a year: you can drive it and enjoy it, but you cannot sell it or wreck it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'usufructuarius,' from 'usufructus,' combining 'usus' (use) and 'fructus' (fruit, enjoyment), from 'frui' (to enjoy).
common_mistakes: Using 'usufructuary' as a general word for any user of a product, when it is a specific legal term about property.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'YOO-zoo-fruk-TOO-ary' instead of stressing the 'fruc' syllable with a reduced ending.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of vocative case.
Abbreviation of verb.
Vagina.
Abbreviation of vowel.
Abbreviation of velocity.
Viagra.
Anything shaped like a V.
A flying skein of geese or other birds which have placed themselves in a V-shaped formation.
Abbreviation of venturi.
senses.example: 4V

core.definition: The twenty-second letter of the English alphabet, also used as an abbreviation for verb, vocative or the Roman numeral five.

pronunciation.tip: Touch your upper teeth to your lower lip and voice the sound 'v', then add a long 'ee'. Do not say 'we' or 'b'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. As a letter or grammar abbreviation, it carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the letter 'V' as 'vee' and use it in everyday spelling, sports (V-neck, V-8 engine) and grammar abbreviations. In legal citations, 'v.' means versus, as in 'Smith v. Jones'. In casual speech, 'vs.' is more common. Avoid the crude slang sense of the letter alone.

distinctions.note: In legal and academic citations, 'v.' means 'versus' and is written with a period, as in 'Brown v. Board'.
In everyday and sports writing, 'vs.' is the common way to write 'versus', as in 'Lakers vs. Celtics'.

examples.everyday: My last name starts with V, so I always get called near the end of the list.
examples.professional: Put the total for each region in column V of the spreadsheet, next to the margin figures.
examples.analytical: In the grammatical notation, V marks the verb phrase, while the Roman numeral V marks the fifth item in the sequence.

nuance.analogy: The letter V is like a tent pole: a simple shape that holds up a lot of meaning.
nuance.etymology: From Latin V, which was used for both the sounds 'u' and 'v'; it descends from Greek upsilon, from Phoenician waw.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'V' as 'we' or 'b'; the sound requires the lower lip and upper teeth.
Confusing 'v.' and 'vs.' in writing; 'v.' is for legal citations, 'vs.' for everyday use.

senses.definition: Random variable.
A measurable quantity capable of taking on a number of values.
A variable, often the set of x values plotted on a graph.
senses.example: In the regression output, the variate on the x-axis was time in months.

senses.definition: The measured magnitude of a variable.
To alter; to vary; to make or become different.
senses.example: Over the years, the recipe would variate with whatever produce the farmers' market had.

core.definition: In statistics, a random variable or a measurable quantity that can take on a range of values.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending is a short "it." As a verb, it is pronounced "VAIR-ee-ayt," so be careful to match the form to the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use variate mainly in statistics and mathematics textbooks, and in papers on probability. Many Americans would say random variable or simply variable instead, since variate is less common in everyday technical use. In the verb sense, it is archaic or literary, so people would more likely say vary.

distinctions.note: Variable is the usual term in statistics and mathematics; variate is more specialized and less common, often used in older or more formal texts.
A random variable is the precise technical name for a variable whose value depends on chance; variate is a shorter term for the same idea in some texts.

examples.everyday: I don't use the word variate much, but my statistics friend uses it to mean a random quantity.
examples.professional: The simulation generates a random variate from the distribution at each step.
examples.analytical: A variate in a probability model is best understood as a function that assigns numerical values to outcomes of a random process.

nuance.analogy: A variate is like a dice roll recorded as a number: the process is uncertain, but each result is a value you can measure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin variatus, past participle of variare, to change.
common_mistakes: Using variate for an everyday variable without a technical purpose, where variable is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the ending as "ayt" when used as a noun.
Confusing the noun and verb pronunciations.

senses.definition: Commanding respect because of age, dignity, character or position.
Worthy of reverence.
senses.example: The venerable professor received a standing ovation at her retirement dinner.

senses.definition: Ancient, antiquated or archaic.
senses.example: The venerable oak in the town square had been there since before the Revolution.

senses.definition: Made sacred especially by religious or historical association.
senses.example: Pilgrims walked for days to reach the venerable shrine of Saint Thomas.

senses.definition: Giving an impression of aged goodness and benevolence.
senses.example: My grandmother had a venerable face, kind eyes, and a voice like warm honey.

core.definition: Deserving respect because of age, wisdom, dignity, character, or long service, especially in a community or institution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, VEN. The second and third syllables are reduced, and the final 'ble' is a syllabic 'l' in American speech, so it sounds like 'bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies respect earned through age, service, or character, and it can sound slightly old-fashioned when used of ordinary people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use venerable for institutions, traditions, and elders: 'a venerable university' or 'a venerable professor.' It is formal and often used in writing or speeches. In casual talk, old or respected is more natural. Be careful when describing things, since venerable can also mean old-fashioned, which may sound odd in praise of a new product.

distinctions.note: Old is neutral and only states age; venerable adds respect and dignity earned over time.
Respected describes general regard, while venerable suggests reverence and a long, honored history.

examples.everyday: That diner has been on Main Street for seventy years, and everyone treats it like a venerable local landmark.
examples.professional: The venerable firm still uses its original review process, which is both its strength and its bottleneck.
examples.analytical: Aquinas calls the tradition venerable because it preserves the wisdom of earlier generations, though he still subjects it to rational examination.

nuance.analogy: A venerable person is like an old oak tree: its age and endurance command respect without any effort to impress.
nuance.etymology: From Latin venerabilis, from venerari, 'to revere'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in vuh-NAIR-uh-bul.
Using venerable for any old object in praise; it implies respect, not just age.

venerable.etymology: From Middle French *vénérable*, from Old French, from Latin *venerabilis*.

senses.definition: To subject to vernalization.

core.definition: To expose seeds, bulbs, or plants to a period of cold so they will flower or set seed sooner, as they would after winter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VUR, and reduce the middle syllable to 'nuh.' The final '-ize' is pronounced like the word 'eyes.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term from agriculture and plant science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in agriculture, horticulture, plant breeding, and research. Gardeners may say 'chill' the bulbs or seeds instead, especially in everyday talk. If you use 'vernalize' in conversation, be ready to explain the cold treatment.

distinctions.note: Chill is an everyday gardening word for putting bulbs or seeds in the cold, while vernalize is the precise technical term for a cold treatment that triggers flowering.
Stratify refers to cold, moist treatment that breaks seed dormancy, while vernalize usually refers to cold exposure that induces flowering in plants.

examples.everyday: The nursery told me to vernalize the tulip bulbs in the fridge for a few weeks before planting.
examples.professional: We vernalized the winter wheat seed lots before the spring trial so the plants would flower on schedule.
examples.analytical: Biennial crops must be vernalized before they will flower in the field, which explains why their life cycle depends on winter.

nuance.analogy: Like sending a seed through a winter it can feel, so it believes spring has arrived.
nuance.etymology: From vernal, from Latin vernalis, 'of spring,' with the suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'ver-NAL-ize,' when the main stress is on the first syllable.
Confusing it with vernacularize, which means something entirely different.

senses.definition: The fine arts as a subject of study or expertise; understanding of arts and antiquities.
senses.example: Her grandfather's collection of Renaissance bronzes earned him a reputation for real virtu.

senses.definition: Objets d'art collectively.
Especially with reference to the writings of Machiavelli (1469–1527): the requisite qualities for political or military success; vitality, determination; power.
senses.example: Machiavelli argued that a prince needs virtu, not just luck, to hold power.

senses.definition: Moral worth; virtue, virtuousness.
senses.example: The old priest spoke often of virtu, the quiet moral worth that outlasts wealth.

core.definition: Appreciation and knowledge of fine arts and antiquities, or the collection of objects valued for their artistic quality.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, 'too', which is a borrowing from Italian. The first syllable is a weak 'ver' with the r pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it sounds learned and refined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this word mainly in art history, museum studies and antiques writing. Most Americans would say 'fine arts', 'antiquities' or 'objects of art' in everyday speech. In Machiavelli scholarship, 'virtù' names political skill or vigor, a sense that is rarely used outside that field.

distinctions.note: 'Virtue' means moral goodness or a good quality of character, while 'virtu' means artistic knowledge or the objects themselves.
A 'virtuoso' is a highly skilled performer, while 'virtu' refers to art knowledge or objects rather than a person's skill.

examples.everyday: At the estate auction, the dealer praised the collection's virtu to the guests.
examples.professional: The curator's catalog entry explains the bronzes' value as objects of virtu from the Renaissance.
examples.analytical: In Machiavelli's writing, virtù names the quality that lets a ruler master fortune, not moral goodness.

nuance.analogy: Virtu is like a museum's sense of taste: knowing what is beautiful, old and valuable.
nuance.etymology: From Italian 'virtù', from Latin 'virtus' (manliness, excellence, courage).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'virtu' with 'virtue', which means moral goodness.
Stressing the first syllable, 'VUR-too', rather than the Italian-style final stress.

senses.definition: To express with the voice, to utter.
To produce noises or calls from the throat.
senses.example: We could hear the monkeys vocalizing, though we could not see them.

senses.definition: To turn a consonant into a vowel.
senses.example: In Hong Kong English, /l/ may be vocalized at the end of a syllable.

senses.definition: To add vowel points to a consonantal script (e.g. niqqud in Hebrew)
senses.example: The scholar vocalized the consonantal text of the psalm using the traditional Masoretic marks.

senses.definition: To sing without using words.
senses.example: The soprano vocalized through the long scale before the first aria began.

senses.definition: (dated) To make a sound voiced rather than voiceless.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To say something out loud, or to make sounds with your voice, especially to express a feeling, opinion or concern.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VOH. The final syllable rhymes with 'rise,' so do not pronounce it as 'eyes-ez' or 'lize' with a long E.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when someone speaks up, or negative when someone expresses anger or complaints loudly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vocalize' for saying concerns or feelings out loud, especially at work, as in 'Please vocalize any concerns now.' In music, singers and teachers say 'vocalize' for warm-up exercises on vowels. It is a bit more formal than 'say' or 'speak up,' so it fits meetings and writing better than casual chat.

distinctions.note: Verbalize means to put thoughts into words, while vocalize emphasizes actually producing sound with the voice.
Voice can mean expressing an opinion in writing or speech, but vocalize specifically means saying it aloud.

examples.everyday: If something about the trip bothers you, go ahead and vocalize it before we book the hotel.
examples.professional: Please vocalize any blockers in the standup so the team can help before the release.
examples.analytical: The author argues that minority communities were often unable to vocalize their grievances within the existing public sphere.

nuance.analogy: Vocalizing an idea is like opening a valve so the pressure inside becomes sound.
nuance.etymology: From vocal plus the suffix -ize, making a verb meaning to make vocal.
common_mistakes: Using vocalize for silent thinking. It requires actual speech or sound.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first, which is VOH-kuh-lyz.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to volume or volumes.
Consisting of many folds, coils, or convolutions.
senses.example: The voluminous folds of the velvet curtain pooled heavily across the stage floor.

senses.definition: Of great volume, or bulk; large.
Having written much, or produced many volumes.
senses.example: a voluminous writer

core.definition: Very large in quantity, size, or volume; taking up a great deal of space.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOO, and the second syllable is a weak schwa. The -ous ending is pronounced like uhs, not a full oo-sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe impressive large amounts or, in a complaint, something overwhelming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use voluminous in formal writing and descriptions of large amounts of text, records, or clothing. In everyday speech they say huge, a lot of, or bulky. It appears often in legal and academic writing, for example voluminous records or voluminous correspondence.

distinctions.note: Large is common and neutral about size; voluminous specifically refers to great volume or bulk, often of papers, fabric, or writing.
Vast emphasizes immense extent or scale, while voluminous stresses a large amount that fills or fills out a space.

examples.everyday: She wore a voluminous coat that made her look twice her size.
examples.professional: The auditors reviewed voluminous transaction logs before they found the duplicated payments.
examples.analytical: Her voluminous footnotes demonstrate a mastery of the sources, but they also distract from the central claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a suitcase stuffed with clothes that barely closes: the amount is large enough to fill the whole space.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin voluminosus, from volumen, roll or volume.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as vuh-LOO-muh-NUS; the -ous ending is weak.
Confusing voluminous with voluptuous, which means curvy or sensually pleasing, not large in amount.

senses.definition: A thin disk of consecrated unleavened bread used in communion.
A light, thin, flat biscuit/cookie.
senses.example: She served lemon wafers alongside the coffee after dinner.

senses.definition: A soft disk originally made of flour, and later of gelatin or a similar substance, used to seal letters, attach papers etc.
senses.example: The notary pressed a red wafer onto each document to make it official.

senses.definition: A thin disk of silicon or other semiconductor on which an electronic circuit is produced.
senses.example: Engineers inspected each silicon wafer for defects before cutting it into individual chips.

senses.definition: To seal or fasten with a wafer.
senses.example: Before mailing the invitations, she wafered each envelope shut with a gold seal.

core.definition: A thin, flat disk of unleavened bread consecrated and eaten during Communion or the Lord's Supper in some churches.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'er' is a light American r-colored vowel. Do not pronounce the 'a' as 'ah'; it is a long 'ay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in church contexts it is sacred, and in food contexts it is a plain, ordinary item.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches, you will hear 'wafer' or 'communion wafer' in Catholic and some Lutheran, Episcopal, or Methodist services. Many Protestant churches use bread cubes or pieces instead. Outside church, Americans use 'wafer' for a thin crisp cookie, such as a vanilla wafer, which is probably the sense you will meet most often in stores.

distinctions.note: In Catholic usage, host is the consecrated bread used in Mass, often a wafer, while wafer is the more general term for the thin disk itself.
A cracker is a dry, usually salty snack, while a wafer is thin and sweet or delicate, and a communion wafer is specifically consecrated.

examples.everyday: At the store, I grabbed a box of vanilla wafers to go with my tea.
examples.professional: Our church ordered communion wafers from a supplier that makes them unleavened and gluten-free.
examples.analytical: In Exodus 29, unleavened wafers anointed with oil are part of the priestly offering, which gives the later Eucharistic wafer a biblical root.

nuance.analogy: A communion wafer is like a thin, plain signpost pointing to a much larger meaning: the simple bread carries the weight of the sacrament.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'waufre,' from Old French 'waufre' or 'gaufre,' a honeycomb-patterned cake or pastry.
common_mistakes: Confusing the communion wafer with the cookie sense in a church conversation; context usually makes it clear.
Pronouncing it 'WAH-fer' with an open a sound instead of the American 'WAY-fer.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word 'raqiq' means a thin cake or wafer, and Exodus 29:2 and Leviticus 8:26 describe unleavened wafers offered in priestly rites. The Greek word 'azymos' means unleavened, and the Gospel accounts of the Last Supper, such as Matthew 26:26, describe Jesus blessing bread, which later Christians connected with wafers. These passages show the ritual background for the wafer used in Communion.

traditions.view: The Church uses unleavened wafer bread, which is consecrated at Mass and believed to become the body of Christ through transubstantiation.
Orthodox churches use leavened bread, prepared as prosphora or similar loaves, and do not use unleavened wafers for the Eucharist.

Practice varies: Lutheran, Anglican, and some Reformed churches often use wafers or bread, while many Baptist and Pentecostal churches use bread cubes or whole loaves and emphasize memorial or spiritual presence rather than transubstantiation.

wafer.etymology: From Middle English *wafre*, from Anglo-Norman *wafre*, *waufre*, from a Germanic source.

senses.definition: To move (something) with short, quick motions; to wobble.
To quickly raise and lower in rapid succession, usually as an implication of slyness, smugness, or suggestiveness.
senses.example: He would waggle his eyebrows whenever he mentioned the new neighbor.

senses.definition: To reel, sway, or move from side to side; to move with a wagging motion; to waddle.
senses.example: The old duck began to waggle along the path toward the pond.

senses.definition: An instance of waggling.
senses.example: With a quick waggle of her finger, she told the kids to stop arguing.

senses.definition: A wobbling motion.
senses.example: Give the cable a waggle to let it come out quicker.

senses.definition: The preliminary swinging of the club head back and forth over the ball in the line of the proposed stroke.
senses.example: Before the putt, he took a few slow waggles to get a feel for the line.

core.definition: To move something back and forth or up and down in quick, short motions, such as a finger, a tail, or a loose tooth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is just the l sound with no extra vowel. Avoid saying 'wag-GEL' with a hard second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, playful in everyday talk. The sense of waggling a finger at someone is mildly scolding, and waggling your eyebrows can suggest flirting or smugness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use waggle for small, playful movements: a dog's tail, a finger shaken at a naughty child, or a golfer's practice swing. It is casual and lighthearted, so it fits everyday conversation and storytelling. In a formal report you would usually say oscillate or vibrate instead.

distinctions.note: Wiggle suggests a livelier, more wriggling motion, often from side to side, while waggle is slower and more deliberate.
Wobble implies instability or unsteadiness, while waggle is an intentional back-and-forth motion.
Wag usually describes a tail or head moving briskly, and it is more strongly tied to animals; waggle can apply to fingers, hands, or objects.

examples.everyday: My little nephew kept waggling his finger at the cat, like he was scolding it.
examples.professional: Before the demo, the presenter waggled the mouse cable to show the loose connection.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the author's ironic phrasing waggles its eyebrows at the reader, inviting a knowing smile rather than a plain claim.

nuance.analogy: Waggle is like a dog's tail: quick, side-to-side, and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: Frequentative of wag, meaning to move back and forth, formed with the -le suffix.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full vowel, like 'WAG-ul-ee'.
Confusing waggle with wiggle, which is livelier and more wriggling.

waggle.etymology: From Middle English *wagelen* (attested in *wagelyng*), possibly a borrowing of *wagelen*; equivalent to *wag* + *le*.

senses.definition: A person who wangles.

core.definition: A person who gets what they want through clever, sneaky, or manipulative methods, often by using connections.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The ending -ler is a rhotic schwa sound, so say 'WANG-gler' with a soft r, not 'WANG-glair'. Do not confuse it with 'wrangler'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to neutral; it can be admiring when describing someone who is skilled at getting things done, but it usually implies a little dishonesty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wangler informally to describe someone who is good at getting favors, tickets, or perks, often with a slight tone of disapproval or amusement. It is rarely used in formal writing. In a workplace, 'operator' or 'a well-connected person' might be more diplomatic. The word is most natural in casual gossip about a friend or colleague.

distinctions.note: A schemer plots deliberately, often to harm others, while a wangler mainly seeks personal favors.
Operator is neutral or positive in business, describing someone who gets results, while wangler carries more suspicion.

examples.everyday: Don't ask Mike for help with tickets; he's the office wangler and always knows someone.
examples.professional: Our procurement lead is a wangler, but she gets us the best vendor terms, so we tolerate her methods.
examples.analytical: The wangler exploits the gap between formal rules and informal favors, which is why institutions struggle to control him.

nuance.analogy: A wangler is like a skilled plumber who finds a hidden pipe to route water where it is needed, though the pipe may not have been meant for that use.
nuance.etymology: From wangle (verb) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing wangler with wrangler, which means a cowboy who handles horses or a person who manages a difficult situation.
Using wangler as a neutral job title in formal writing, where it sounds too casual.

senses.definition: To parry, or turn aside.
senses.example: He raised his arms to ward off the attack.

senses.definition: To, while in possession of the ball, move the free hand or the hand and arm holding the butt end of the stick laterally into a defending player's body or stick.
senses.example: In lacrosse, he wards off the defender with his free arm while cradling the ball.

senses.definition: To avert or prevent.
senses.example: He wore garlic to ward off vampires.

core.definition: To prevent or keep away something harmful or unpleasant, such as illness, danger, or an attack.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'off' most strongly. In fast speech, 'ward off' links into something like 'wor-DAWF.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, describing protection or prevention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ward off' in everyday talk about colds, infections, pests, and worries, as in 'take vitamin C to ward off a cold.' It is also common in news and business writing about threats. For a more casual feel, Americans might say 'keep away' or 'fight off.'

distinctions.note: Fend off usually means resisting something that is already attacking you, while ward off often means preventing something before it arrives.
Prevent is neutral and formal, while ward off is more active and vivid, suggesting you are keeping something at bay.

examples.everyday: Take some vitamin C to ward off the cold before the trip.
examples.professional: We added monitoring alerts to ward off outages before they reach customers.
examples.analytical: Many ancient cultures wore amulets to ward off the evil eye, believing protection could be carried in objects.

nuance.analogy: Ward off is like holding up an umbrella before the rain starts, keeping the trouble from reaching you.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'ward' (to guard) plus the adverb 'off.'
common_mistakes: Using 'warn off' when you mean 'ward off,' since 'warn off' means to alert someone to stay away.
Adding a preposition such as 'ward off from,' when the verb takes the threat directly as its object.

senses.definition: To help to swallow (something, especially food or a pill) by drinking a liquid.
senses.example: Now we just need a drink to wash it down.

senses.definition: To wash (something) completely from top to bottom.
senses.example: You must wash the wall down well before painting.

senses.definition: To send (something) down the drain by washing action.
senses.example: There was some food residue in the sink, so she washed it down.

core.definition: To help swallow food or a pill by drinking a liquid, or to clean something thoroughly from top to bottom.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short o sound in 'wash', the American cot vowel, and stress 'down' as the main word. Link the phrase so it sounds like 'wahsh-DOWN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes everyday actions like taking medicine or cleaning a surface.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'wash down' most often for pills or food, as in 'He washed down the pills with a glass of water.' For cleaning, people more often say 'hose down' or 'scrub down' for surfaces. Note that 'wash down' is informal and mostly spoken, so in writing people may choose 'swallow' or 'clean.'

distinctions.note: Swallow only means to take food or liquid into the throat, while wash down adds the idea of drinking a liquid to help it go down.
Hose down means spraying with water from a hose, while wash down can mean cleaning by any washing action.

examples.everyday: I took two ibuprofen and washed them down with a big glass of water.
examples.professional: Before the client visit, the cleaning crew washed down the conference room and the glass walls.
examples.analytical: The phrasal verb 'wash down' combines the idea of cleansing with the sense of helping something pass down the throat.

nuance.analogy: Washing down a pill is like sending a bus down a road with a flood of water: the liquid carries the solid along.
nuance.etymology: 'Wash' from Old English 'wascan' plus 'down', meaning from a higher place to a lower one.
common_mistakes: Using 'wash down' without an object, like 'He washed down' with no pill or food named.
Confusing the particle: 'wash down' is not 'wash up' for cleaning dishes in American speech.

conversation.text: He washed down his burger with a big soda.
I need something to wash down this spicy food.
She washed the pill down with some water.

senses.definition: A social gathering for the purpose of watching a specific event or program on television.
senses.example: We're hosting a watch party for the season finale at our place on Sunday night.

core.definition: A social gathering where friends get together to watch a TV show, game or event on screen.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PAR in 'party', with a lighter stress on 'watch'. The r is pronounced in American English, and the t often sounds like a soft d in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fun, friendship and a shared experience.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in American life, especially for the Super Bowl, season finales and awards shows like the Oscars. Hosts often say 'Come over and watch the game', and 'watch party' is the term when it is organized around a broadcast or streaming event. A natural reply is 'Sounds fun, what should I bring?'

distinctions.note: Watch party is the everyday term; viewing party is slightly more formal and is more common in film or marketing contexts.
A potluck is about sharing food; a watch party is about watching something together, though food is often shared.

examples.everyday: We're hosting a watch party for the season finale on Sunday, so bring some snacks.
examples.professional: Marketing organized a watch party for the product launch video so the team could react together.
examples.analytical: A watch party turns passive viewing into a shared ritual, where the audience's reactions become part of the event.

nuance.analogy: Like a campfire: people gather around a shared light, and the experience grows because it is shared.
nuance.etymology: Compound of watch (Old English wæcce) and party (from Old French partie).
common_mistakes: Writing 'watch-party' with a hyphen in everyday writing; the usual form is two words.
Saying 'watching party' instead of 'watch party'.
Mispronouncing 'party' as 'PAR-tee' with a hard t sound; the American t is often soft and flapped.

senses.definition: A translucent design impressed on the surface of paper and visible when the paper is held to the light.
A logo superimposed on a digital image, a television broadcast, etc.
senses.example: The stock photos on our site carry a faint watermark in the corner.

senses.definition: A value stored in a datafile to ensure its integrity, so that if the file's contents are changed then the watermark will no longer match the contents.
senses.example: The software checks the file's watermark before loading it, rejecting any tampered data.

senses.definition: A default hint caption displayed in a text box prior to the user inputting any text.
senses.example: The search box still shows a gray watermark reading Enter your email address.

senses.definition: A mark indicating the level to which water has risen.
senses.example: The old bridge piling had a watermark showing where the flood reached in 1952.

senses.definition: To mark paper with a watermark.
senses.example: The mill watermarks its premium stationery with the company's crest.

senses.definition: To mark a datafile with a digital watermark.
senses.example: The studio watermarks every preview clip before sending it to clients.

core.definition: A faint design pressed into paper, visible when held up to light; also a hidden digital code embedded in a file or image to show its origin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle light, with a flapped t. The final syllable has a clear r, so say /ɑɹk/ with the tongue curled, not 'mahk'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical or descriptive term that can signal authenticity or ownership.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, watermark usually refers to a faint design in paper, like the one on a banknote or check. In digital contexts, it means a logo or code overlaid on images or video to show ownership. Americans use it in both senses in tech, media and design work.

distinctions.note: A logo is a brand symbol shown openly, while a watermark is usually faint or hidden and used to show authenticity or ownership.
A signature is a handwritten or typed name, while a watermark is a design or code built into the material itself.

collocations: hold it up to the light to see the watermark

examples.everyday: Hold the bill up to the light and you can see the watermark.
examples.professional: We added a visible watermark to the draft images so clients can't use them before final approval.
examples.analytical: A digital watermark makes a claim about provenance, but it proves little if the embedding method itself can be removed or forged.

nuance.analogy: Like a faint signature built into the paper itself, visible only when you hold it up to the light.
nuance.etymology: Compound of water and mark; the design was first made by the wire pattern of the paper mold.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'watermelon' or with a flood line, which Americans call a high-water mark.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a strong 'tar' instead of a light flapped t.

senses.definition: Lacking in force (usually strength) or ability.
senses.example: The child was too weak to move the boulder.

senses.definition: Unable to sustain a great weight, pressure, or strain.
senses.example: a weak timber; a weak rope

senses.definition: Limp, soft.
senses.example: The tomato had gone weak and mushy after sitting in the fridge for a week.

senses.definition: Unable to withstand temptation, urgency, persuasion, etc. easily impressed, moved, or overcome; accessible; vulnerable.
senses.example: weak resolutions; weak virtue

senses.definition: Having a strong, irrepressible emotional love for someone or (less often) something; sentimentally affected by such love.
senses.example: Grandpa was weak for his grandchildren and spoiled them with candy every Sunday.

senses.definition: Dilute, lacking in taste or potency.
senses.example: We were served stale bread and weak tea.

senses.definition: English Wikipedia has an article on:Weak inflectionWikipedia Displaying a particular kind of inflection.
senses.example: The verb to walk is weak because it has a past tense of walked and all forms are inflected by adding the typical suffix (ie is regular) to the stem walk- (ie has no vowel changes).

senses.definition: Regular in inflection, lacking vowel changes and having a past tense marked by /-d-/, /-t-/, or /-ð-/.
senses.example: The verb to walk is weak because it has a past tense of walked and all forms are inflected by adding the typical suffix (ie is regular) to the stem walk- (ie has no vowel changes).

senses.definition: Showing less distinct grammatical endings.
senses.example: In German, weak adjectives take endings that differ from strong ones after definite articles.

senses.definition: Definite in meaning, often used with a definite article or similar word.
senses.example: Old English used the weak form of the adjective after a demonstrative like this.

senses.definition: Related to, containing, or being a consonant which is prone to disappearing in some inflections, in most applicable languages including (but not limited to) w and y.
senses.example: In some Semitic languages such as Akkadian, some or all gutturals are weak and often disappear, but in others such as Arabic and Ugaritic, they are strong and never disappear.

senses.definition: Related to, being, or containing the lenis consonant gradation, which resulted from historically closed syllables.
senses.example: The Finnish verb kääntää (“to translate”) inflects to the singular imperative as käännä, showing the weak gradation nt > nn because it historically ended in a consonant which closed the syllable.

senses.definition: Of a form in which the accent tends to shift forwards (to the right, in transcription) or did so ancestrally in Proto-Indo-European, relative to the strong stem (which has the leftmost accent allowed).
senses.example: The PIE zero grade was most often found in weak stems, such as in *mn̥téys (“of thought, from thinking”, genitive/ablative singular of *méntis) and *mn̥yóh₂er (“I am thinking”). Over time it spread to strong stems, i.e. *mń̥tis, by processes of analogy and leveling. The full grade was persistent in the first syllable of reduplicated stative verbs: strong *tetórph₂e (“I am satisfied”), weak *tetr̥pmé (“we all are satisfied”), though for some verbs such as *pí-ph₃-e- (“to drink”) there was an unusual i-grade which may have lacked any distinct weak counterpart.

senses.definition: In a grammatical case other than nominative, accusative, vocative or sometimes locative singular.
senses.example: In that grammar, the weak genitive and dative forms are identical for most masculine nouns.

senses.definition: In a conjugation other than singular active forms (regardless of person, tense etc.).
senses.example: All middle forms of Indo-European verbs are traditionally weak. Middle-only verbs can still be compared to hypothetical strong stems, such as weak *ǵn̥h₁-yé- (e.g. *ǵn̥h₁yéto, “(he/she/it) was born”) versus strong *ǵénh₁-ye-.

senses.definition: Lenis, pronounced with less force or less markedness.
senses.example: In many dialects of English, the t in city is pronounced weak, almost like a flap.

senses.definition: Bad or uncool.
senses.example: This place is weak.

senses.definition: Having a narrow range of logical consequences; narrowly applicable. (Often contrasted with a strong statement which implies it.)
senses.example: The theorem is weak because it assumes far less than the stronger version.

senses.definition: Resulting from, or indicating, lack of judgment, discernment, or firmness; unwise; hence, foolish.
senses.example: Giving him your password was a weak decision, and the scammers exploited it immediately.

senses.definition: Not having power to convince; not supported by force of reason or truth; unsustained.
senses.example: The prosecution advanced a weak case.

senses.definition: Lacking in vigor or expression.
senses.example: a weak sentence; a weak style

senses.definition: Not prevalent or effective, or not felt to be prevalent; not potent; feeble.
senses.example: The coffee tasted weak, so I asked the barista for an extra shot.

senses.definition: Tending towards lower prices.
senses.example: a weak market; wheat is weak at present

senses.definition: Lacking contrast.
senses.example: a weak negative

senses.definition: That does not ionize completely into anions and cations in a solution.
senses.example: a weak acid

senses.definition: One of the four fundamental forces associated with nuclear decay.
senses.example: The weak interaction is responsible for certain kinds of radioactive beta decay.

core.definition: Lacking physical strength or power; unable to lift, carry, or resist much force.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long EE vowel, the same as 'week'. End with a clean k and do not add a vowel after it, so it is not 'weak-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative when applied to a person's character, since calling someone weak is an insult. It is neutral for coffee, tea, or a signal, where it means mild or faint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'weak' for people, muscles, coffee, signals, and arguments. Calling a person weak is blunt, so in conversation people often say 'not strong' or 'a little frail' instead. For a weak cup of coffee, Americans mean it is too diluted, not that it is bad.

distinctions.note: Feeble suggests very little strength, often pitiful or from old age; weak is the general everyday word.
Fragile describes things that break easily; weak can describe a person's ability, a structure, or an argument.
Frail implies physical delicacy from age or illness; weak is broader and can describe ideas as well as bodies.

examples.everyday: This coffee tastes a little weak, so could you make it stronger?
examples.professional: The sales forecast looks weak for the third quarter, so we should revisit our assumptions.
examples.analytical: The argument is weak because its central premise assumes the very conclusion it needs to prove.

nuance.analogy: A weak bridge is like one built with thin beams: it looks fine until the load arrives.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wāc, meaning pliant, soft, or yielding, from a root sense of bending easily.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'weak' with 'week'; both are pronounced /wik/ but mean different things.
Using 'weak' for a diluted drink as if it were bad; Americans mean it is too thin in flavor.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is asthenes (ἀσθενής), meaning without strength, weak, or sick. Paul uses weakness as the place where God's strength is seen. 1 Corinthians 1:27 says God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong. Romans 15:1 says the strong ought to bear with the failings of the weak rather than please themselves.

weak.etymology: From Middle English *waik*, *wayk*, *wayke*, *weik*, *weyk*, borrowed from Old Norse *veikr* (“weak”), from Proto-Germanic **waikwaz* (“weak, yielded, pliant, bendsome”), from **wīkwaną* (“to cease, fold, yield; to retreat”), from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: To have on:
senses.example: He's wearing some nice pants today.

senses.definition: To carry or have equipped on or about one's body, as an item of clothing, equipment, decoration, perfume, etc.
senses.example: He's wearing some nice pants today.

senses.definition: To have or carry on one's person habitually, consistently; or, to maintain in a particular fashion or manner.
senses.example: He wears eyeglasses.

senses.definition: To bear or display in one's aspect or appearance.
senses.example: She wore a smile all day.

senses.definition: To erode:
senses.example: You're going to wear a hole in the bottom of those shoes.

senses.definition: To eat away at, erode, diminish, or consume gradually; to cause a gradual deterioration in; to produce (some change) through attrition, exposure, or constant use.
senses.example: You're going to wear a hole in the bottom of those shoes.

senses.definition: To undergo gradual deterioration; become impaired; be reduced or consumed gradually due to any continued process, activity, or use.
senses.example: The tiles were wearing thin due to years of children's feet.

senses.definition: To exhaust, fatigue, expend, or weary.
senses.example: His neverending criticism has finally worn my patience.

senses.definition: (in the phrase "wearing on (someone)") To cause annoyance, irritation, fatigue, or weariness near the point of an exhaustion of patience.
senses.example: Her high pitched voice is really wearing on me lately.

senses.definition: To endure:
senses.example: I know you don't like working with him, but you'll just have to wear it.

senses.definition: To overcome one's reluctance and endure a (previously specified) situation.
senses.example: I know you don't like working with him, but you'll just have to wear it.

senses.definition: To last or remain durable under hard use or over time; to retain usefulness, value, or desirable qualities under any continued strain or long period of time; sometimes said of a person, regarding the quality of being easy or difficult to tolerate.
senses.example: Don't worry, this fabric will wear. These pants will last you for years.

senses.definition: To pass slowly, gradually or tediously.
senses.example: wear on, wear away.

senses.definition: To bring (a sailing vessel) onto the other tack by bringing the wind around the stern (as opposed to tacking when the wind is brought around the bow); to come round on another tack by turning away from the wind.
senses.example: The captain ordered the crew to wear the ship around, keeping clear of the reef.

senses.definition: Clothing.
senses.example: footwear; outdoor wear; maternity wear

senses.definition: Damage to the appearance and/or strength of an item caused by use over time.
senses.example: The tires showed heavy wear after only two years of driving on gravel roads.

senses.definition: Fashion.
senses.example: The designer's spring wear was all oversized blazers and soft linen trousers.

senses.definition: Wearing.
senses.example: Daily wear of the sandals left the leather soft and comfortable.

core.definition: To have clothing, jewelry, glasses, or other items on your body, or to regularly carry something with you.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the same as in 'hair' and 'bear', not the long e of 'we'. The r is pronounced clearly in American speech, so don't drop it. Avoid saying 'we-er', which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes everyday choices about clothing and style and rarely carries strong emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wear' for clothes, shoes, glasses, watches, and jewelry, and they often ask 'What should I wear?' or say 'Wear something comfortable.' For wearing a substance such as perfume or makeup, Americans also say 'wear perfume' or 'wear makeup.' In formal writing 'wear' can also describe a habit or manner of behaving, as in 'wear a smile'.

distinctions.note: 'Put on' describes the action of dressing, while 'wear' describes the state of having something on.
'Dress' can mean to put on clothes or to be dressed in a certain style, and it is often used for dressing up, while 'wear' is more general.
'Carry' means to hold or transport something, while 'wear' refers to items on the body, not in your hands or bag.

examples.everyday: What should I wear to the wedding, a suit or something more casual?
examples.professional: Please wear your company badge at all times while you are in the building.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of dress have argued that what we wear communicates social identity, beyond the simple function of covering the body.

nuance.analogy: Wearing something is like carrying a message on your body that others can read at a glance.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'werian', meaning to clothe or cover.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'wear' as 'we-er', which confuses it with 'where' and 'weer'. The American sound is closer to 'hair'.
Confusing 'wear' with 'where' in speech. Context usually makes it clear, but the pronunciation difference matters in conversation.

wear.etymology: Middle English *weren*, from Old English *werian* (“to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock”), from **waʀjan*, from Proto-Germanic **wazjaną* (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European **wes-* (“to dress, put on”).

senses.definition: In a weary manner; feeling weary.
senses.example: He sat down wearily after twelve hours of debugging the pipeline.

senses.definition: In a weary manner; causing weariness.
senses.example: The sermon droned on wearily, each point repeated until the pews grew restless.

core.definition: In a tired, exhausted way, with little energy or enthusiasm, often after long effort or frustration.

pronunciation.tip: The spelling suggests the vowel of 'wear', but the first syllable has the short i of 'wiry' followed by r. The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ly is pronounced 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It conveys fatigue, sometimes resignation or boredom.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wearily' in stories, news reports and everyday descriptions of people who are exhausted, such as 'she sighed wearily'. It describes manner rather than simple tiredness, so it fits after long days or repeated disappointments. In speech people more often say 'tiredly' or 'with a sigh', so 'wearily' sounds a bit more written.

distinctions.note: Tiredly often refers to sleepiness or physical fatigue, while wearily suggests exhaustion from prolonged strain, frustration or boredom.

examples.everyday: She sighed wearily and said, 'Fine, I'll drive.'
examples.professional: He admitted wearily in the standup that the migration had slipped another two weeks.
examples.analytical: Pascal's wearily resigned reflections on human restlessness show how boredom can drive the search for distraction.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone battery at two percent, a person who moves wearily is running on the last of their energy.
nuance.etymology: From weary (Old English wērig) plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable with the vowel of 'wear' (WAIR-ih-lee).
Confusing 'wearily' with 'weirdly' in speech and writing.

senses.definition: A gentle neigh.
senses.example: The horse let out a soft whinny when it saw the carrot in my hand.

senses.definition: To make a gentle neigh.

core.definition: To make a soft, gentle neighing sound, as a horse does when it greets someone or feels calm.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables, stressed on the first: WIN-ee. The short i is like 'win', not 'wine'. The second syllable is a bright 'ee', not 'nigh'. Don't confuse it with 'whiny', which has a different vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes a gentle, friendly sound, usually from a horse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'whinny' almost only for horses. For a louder or more general horse sound, they say 'neigh'. In everyday talk, you might say 'the horse whinnied when it saw me', and it sounds natural and warm.

distinctions.note: Neigh is the louder, more general word for a horse's cry; whinny is softer and friendlier.
Nicker is a low, soft sound horses make to greet people; whinny is higher and can express excitement or distress.
Whiny is an adjective for complaining; whinny is a horse's sound, and the vowels differ.

examples.everyday: The horse gave a soft whinny when it saw the carrot in my hand.
examples.professional: Our vet's report says the new horse whinnies whenever the barn door opens.
examples.analytical: The poem's whinny at dawn is less a sound than a symbol of longing for the wild.

nuance.analogy: A whinny is like a friendly hello from a horse: soft, warm, and meant for someone nearby.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of the sound a horse makes.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'whinny' with 'whiny', which means complaining; the vowels and meanings differ.
Using 'whinny' for a loud horse sound, where 'neigh' is more natural.

senses.definition: To relax; to get rid of stress; to destress.
senses.example: After a long day at work, she winds down by kickboxing.

senses.definition: To shut down slowly (by degrees or in phases).
senses.example: A program as complex as the Space Shuttle program takes some time to wind down.

senses.definition: To lower by winding, as with a crank or windlass.
senses.example: Wind down the car window if you want to talk to me.

senses.definition: To unwind.
senses.example: You'd better wind down that wind-up toy before you take it apart, or pieces might go flying.

senses.definition: To slow, as if coming to an end; to become calmer or less busy.
senses.example: The festival seems to be winding down now.

core.definition: To gradually relax after a busy or stressful time, or to slowly reduce activity until it stops.

pronunciation.tip: Wind rhymes with 'mind', with a long i, not the wind that blows. The main stress is on down, so say wynd DOWN. The d at the end of wind is quick, and the two words link smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes calming down, though it can also describe a slow decline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in everyday conversation: 'I need to wind down after work.' A common reply is 'Good idea, take it easy.' It can also describe a business or project slowing down, as in 'the company is winding down operations.' It is informal, so in formal writing use 'wind down' only for gradual reduction.

distinctions.note: Relax is general and can describe any rest; wind down suggests a gradual transition from activity to rest.
Unwind is a very close synonym in American speech and is equally common for relaxing after work.
Slow down describes reducing speed; wind down suggests a gradual calming or ending, often over time.

examples.everyday: After the kids are asleep, I like to wind down with a cup of tea and a book.
examples.professional: We will start to wind down the old server in phases over the next two weeks.
examples.analytical: The narrative slowly winds down after the climax, allowing the characters to reflect on what they have lost.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock slowly running down after its spring has been released, moving more and more gently until it stops.
nuance.etymology: Wind from Old English windan, to turn or twist; the phrasal verb is an English combination.
common_mistakes: Using it as one word or with 'up' by mistake; 'wind down' and 'wind up' have different meanings.
Pronouncing wind with a short i like the weather; here it rhymes with 'mind'.

conversation.text: I like to read before bed to wind down.
The party started winding down around midnight.
The company is winding down its operations in Europe.
How do you wind down after a stressful day?

senses.definition: Having no windows, especially no external windows.

core.definition: Having no windows, especially no windows in an outside wall.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WIN. The final -less is a weak, short 'lus' with no strong vowel, and the middle syllable keeps the 'oh' of window.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests a room that feels closed off, dull, or confined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use windowless for offices, server rooms, basements, and vans, often when describing a place's feel or safety concerns. In casual speech, people may say 'no windows' instead. In news reports, windowless van is a common phrase.

distinctions.note: Windowless describes the absence of windows, while dark describes low light, which a room with windows can still have.
Enclosed describes a space shut in by walls, while windowless specifically describes the lack of openings for light and view.

examples.everyday: The break room is windowless, so I always lose track of what the weather is doing.
examples.professional: Our server room is windowless, which keeps the temperature stable but makes it easy to lose track of time.
examples.analytical: A windowless prison cell can strip a person of any sense of time, which is why solitary confinement is so harshly criticized.

nuance.analogy: It is like a room with walls but no eyes, shut off from outside light and view.
nuance.etymology: From window and the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable instead of the first
Assuming windowless means dark, when a room with no windows can still be brightly lit

senses.definition: A cover for a microphone to exclude airy noises such as wind and breathing.
A draught screen at the side of a passenger train doorway.
senses.example: A cold draft blew through the train door until the windscreen was closed.

senses.definition: A lightweight aerodynamic fairing mounted on the nose of an armor-piercing shell to reduce drag and increase range.
senses.example: The shell's windscreen reduced drag and let it travel much farther.

senses.definition: To install a windscreen on.
senses.example: The mechanic windscreened the trailer to cut wind resistance on the highway.

core.definition: A foam or fur cover that fits over a microphone to reduce noise from wind and breathing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WIND. The sk is one quick cluster, and the r in 'screen' is American, so say the word with a clear r before the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a practical audio accessory.
nuance.usage_note: In American audio work, windscreen is common for the microphone cover, and people may also call it a windjammer or dead cat informally. For a car, Americans say windshield, while windscreen is mainly British. Windscreen is also rarely used as a verb, so American speakers usually say put a windscreen on the mic.

distinctions.note: Windshield is the standard American word for a car's front glass, while windscreen is the audio term for a microphone cover.
A pop filter blocks sudden bursts of air from p and b sounds, while a windscreen mainly reduces noise from moving air.

collocations: put a windscreen on the mic

examples.everyday: My friend asked me to bring a windscreen, because the outdoor podcast recording was going to be noisy.
examples.professional: Please add a windscreen to the field mic before we record the interviews on the rooftop.
examples.analytical: Field recordists treat the windscreen as an acoustic filter, since its foam changes the signal before it reaches the preamp.

nuance.analogy: It is like a soft hat on a microphone, keeping gusts from hitting the sensitive part.
nuance.etymology: From wind and screen, meaning something that shields against wind.
common_mistakes: Saying windscreen for a car in American English, where windshield is normal
Using windscreen as a verb in everyday American speech, where a longer phrase is clearer

senses.definition: An appendage of an animal's (bird, bat, insect) body that enables it to fly.
senses.example: The bird was flapping its wings

senses.definition: A fin at the side of a ray or similar fish.
senses.example: The ray glided along the sandy bottom, flapping its broad wing through the water.

senses.definition: Human arm.
senses.example: He tucked the package under his wing as he walked up the steps.

senses.definition: Part of an aircraft that produces the lift for rising into the air.
senses.example: I took my seat on the plane, overlooking the wing.

senses.definition: One of the large pectoral fins of a flying fish.
senses.example: The flying fish launched itself from the waves, spreading its enormous wings.

senses.definition: One of the broad, thin, anterior lobes of the foot of a pteropod, used as an organ in swimming.
senses.example: The sea butterfly beats its wings to swim through the cold Arctic water.

senses.definition: A side shoot of a tree or plant; a branch growing up by the side of another.
senses.example: A new wing sprouted from the side of the rose bush after the spring rain.

senses.definition: Passage by flying; flight.
senses.example: to take wing

senses.definition: Limb or instrument of flight; means of flight or of rapid motion.
senses.example: Her new airline gave the small company the wings it needed to expand quickly.

senses.definition: A part of something that is lesser in size than the main body, and located at the side, such as an extension from the main building.
senses.example: the west wing of the hospital

senses.definition: Either of two similar parts of something.
senses.example: The house has a wing on each side, one for the kitchen and one for the garage.

senses.definition: One of the longer sides of crownworks or hornworks in fortification.
senses.example: The engineers strengthened the long wing of the hornwork before the siege began.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of prison wing, a cellblock; or prison or doing time by extension.

Anything that agitates the air as a wing does, or is put in winglike motion by the action of the air, such as a fan or vane for winnowing grain, the vane or sail of a windmill, the sail of a ship, etc.
senses.example: The old windmill's wing turned slowly in the breeze over the wheat field.

senses.definition: A protruding piece of material on a menstrual pad or diaper to hold it in place and prevent leakage.
senses.example: The new pads have wings that fold around the underwear to prevent leaks.

senses.definition: An ornament worn on the shoulder; a small epaulet or shoulder knot.
senses.example: The general's dress uniform had gold wings on the shoulders.

senses.definition: A cosmetic effect where eyeliner curves outward and ends at a point.
senses.example: She drew a sharp wing at the outer corner of each eye before the wedding.

senses.definition: A faction of a political movement. Usually implies a position apart from the mainstream center position.
senses.example: The more radical wing of the party pushed for a full repeal of the tax.

senses.definition: An organizational grouping in a military aviation service:
senses.example: After the reorganization, his squadron was reassigned to a new wing stationed in Ohio.

senses.definition: A larger formation of two or more groups, which in turn control two or more squadrons.
senses.example: The wing commander reviewed reports from all four squadrons under her command.

senses.definition: One of the unseen areas on the side of the stage in a theater.
senses.example: Between scenes, the actors waited in the wings, ready for their cue.

senses.definition: The insignia of a qualified pilot or aircrew member.
A portable shelter consisting of a fabric roof on a frame, like a tent without sides.
On the enneagram, one of the two adjacent types to an enneatype that forms an individual's subtype of his or her enneatype.
senses.example: Tom's a 4 on the enneagram, with a 3 wing.

senses.definition: A group of plover.
Any membranaceous expansion, such as that along the sides of certain stems, or one of the bracts on a dragon fruit, or of a fruit of the kind called samara.
Either of the two side petals of a papilionaceous flower.
A platform on either side of the bridge of a vessel, normally found in pairs.
That part of the hold or orlop of a vessel which is nearest the sides. In a fleet, one of the extremities when the ships are drawn up in line, or when forming the two sides of a triangle.
A position in several field games on either side of the field.
senses.example: Smith started the game in the center of midfield, but moved to the wing after 30 minutes.

senses.definition: A player occupying such a position; a winger.
(rare) A háček.
senses.label: rare
