senses.definition: To injure slightly (as with a gunshot), especially in the wing or arm.
To fly.
To travel swiftly.
To add a wing (extra part) to.
To act or speak extemporaneously; to improvise; to wing it.
senses.example: I lost all my notes I'd made, so was partially winging the meeting.

senses.definition: To throw.
To furnish with wings.
To transport with, or as if with, wings; to bear in flight, or speedily.
To traverse by flying.

core.definition: One of the two body parts a bird, bat or insect uses to fly; in human contexts, a side part of a building or an arm-like extension.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, relaxed vowel like the i in 'sit'. End with the ng sound only; don't add a hard g as in 'wing-guh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Figurative uses such as 'the left wing' of a political party or 'in the wings' are neutral to slightly formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wing' for animal and airplane wings, and also for sections of buildings, hospitals, stages and political parties. The sense of a human arm is rare and mostly literary or dated in American English. In sports, a winger is a player on the side of the field, and 'on the wing' can describe a position on the side.

distinctions.note: A wing is used for flying, while a fin is used by fish and aquatic animals for swimming and steering.
A feather is one of the light structures covering a wing; the wing is the whole limb that supports flight.

examples.everyday: The sparrow flapped its wings and flew right over the fence.
examples.professional: The engineering team measured the wing span before finalizing the drone's design.
examples.analytical: The wing is a structure whose shape balances lift and drag, which is why flight depends on geometry as much as on muscle.

nuance.analogy: A wing works like a curved sail for the air: moving air pushes it upward, carrying the body along.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'wenge', from Old Norse 'vængr', meaning wing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'weeng' with a long vowel.
Adding a hard g sound after the final ng.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, the word is kanaf (כָּנָף), meaning wing, edge or corner of a garment; in Greek it is pteryx (πτέρυξ), a wing. Isaiah 40:31 (RSV) describes those who wait on the Lord mounting up with wings like eagles, a picture of renewed strength. Psalm 91:4 (RSV) describes God covering the faithful with his pinions, offering them refuge under his wings, a picture of protection. Malachi 4:2 (RSV) speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings.

wing.etymology: From Middle English *winge*, *wenge*, from Old Norse *vængr*, from Proto-Germanic **wēingijaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₂weh₁-* (“to blow”), thus related to *wind*.

senses.definition: In the inner part, spatially; physically inside.
senses.example: within her studio

senses.definition: In the scope or range of.
senses.example: within his hearing; her within five seconds of breaking the record; within an inch of falling overboard

senses.definition: Before the specified duration ends.
senses.example: Leave here within three days.

senses.definition: In or into the interior; inside.
In the context of which the present document or ruling is made.
senses.example: the within appeal

core.definition: Inside the limits or boundaries of something, or inside a range or period of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The th is voiced, like 'this', and the final n is clear; avoid a full second vowel in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use within constantly in everyday and business talk, as in within walking distance, within your budget or within two weeks. It sounds slightly formal in casual speech, where people often say in or inside for physical location. With time and range, however, within is very natural.

distinctions.note: Inside is the everyday word for physical location; within suggests being contained in a limit, range or time frame.
In is broader and more common; within adds the idea of a boundary, as in within the deadline.

examples.everyday: We live within walking distance of the park, so we go there almost every day.
examples.professional: Please send the revised slides within two business days so we can review them before the meeting.
examples.analytical: Within the framework of classical logic, a valid argument cannot have true premises and a false conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a fenced yard: you can move freely inside it, but not beyond the fence.
nuance.etymology: From Old English withinnan, from wið meaning against, plus innan meaning inside.
common_mistakes: Confusing within with without because the words look alike; within means inside, without means lacking
Pronouncing the th as unvoiced, as in 'with', when within has a voiced th

within.etymology: From Middle English *withinne*, *withinnen*, from Old English *wiþinnan*; equivalent to *with* + *in*.

senses.definition: A product of the fine arts; a painting, sculpture, etc.
senses.example: The curator said the painting was a genuine work of art, not a copy.

senses.definition: Anything beautiful, exquisite, or finely crafted.
senses.example: Her handmade quilt is a work of art that took three years to finish.

core.definition: A painting, sculpture, photograph, or other creation made as fine art.

pronunciation.tip: 'Work' gets a light secondary stress and 'art' gets the main stress. 'Of' reduces to 'uhv,' with the f sounding like v, and the r in 'art' is strongly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive. The phrase praises a piece of visual art and can also be used playfully for something beautifully made.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'work of art' for paintings, sculptures, and similar pieces in museums and galleries. In casual talk, people use it to praise something beautifully made, such as a cake or a well-designed website. The phrase can be used ironically, so tone matters.

distinctions.note: Artwork is a general, often informal word for visual art or the images in a design; 'work of art' is more specific and more admiring.
A masterpiece is the greatest work of an artist or period; a work of art can be any good piece of art.
A piece is a neutral, general word for an item of art or craft; 'work of art' emphasizes its quality or beauty.

collocations: a work of art in its own right
a work of art worth millions

examples.everyday: That birthday cake you made is a work of art, and I almost didn't want to cut it.
examples.professional: The client wants the packaging to be a work of art, so the design team will spend two more days on the illustrations.
examples.analytical: Whether a machine-generated image can be a work of art depends on what we think authorship and intention require.

nuance.analogy: A work of art is like a well-made bridge: it does something useful, but people admire it for its design and beauty too.
nuance.etymology: Work from Old English weorc; art from Latin ars, skill or craft.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a work of arts' with a plural 'arts'; the phrase is singular 'work of art.'
Using 'work of art' for any picture or drawing; ordinary sketches or posters are not usually called works of art.

senses.definition: Operation; action.
senses.example: The working of the new machine was explained in the manual's first chapter.

senses.definition: Method of operation.
senses.example: Engineers debated the working of the valve, which determines the pressure.

senses.definition: The incidental or subsidiary calculations performed in solving an overall problem.
senses.example: Be sure to check your working.

senses.definition: Fermentation.
senses.example: The working of the cider took three weeks in the cellar.

senses.definition: (of bodies of water) Becoming full of a vegetable substance.
senses.example: Because of the working in the pond, swimming was banned all summer.

senses.definition: A place where work is carried on.
senses.example: the abandoned mine workings

senses.definition: A train movement.
senses.example: The dispatcher reported a working on the freight line, delaying all afternoon trains.

senses.definition: That is or are functioning.
senses.example: a working ventilator

senses.definition: That suffices but requires additional work; provisional.
senses.example: a working copy of the script

senses.definition: In paid employment.
senses.example: Working mothers have recently joined the factory's workforce.

senses.definition: Of or relating to employment.
senses.example: the working week

senses.definition: Enough to allow one to use something.
senses.example: have a working knowledge of computers

senses.definition: Used in real life; practical.
senses.example: The working minimum focus distance is the distance from the closest focusable subject to the lens.

core.definition: Functioning correctly or able to operate; in good working order, as a device or system is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WURK, with a clear American r. The -ing ending is the velar /ɪŋ/, so do not finish it with a hard n sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive: it describes practical function. 'A working relationship' is polite and neutral, while 'a working theory' means provisional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Is the printer working?' or 'The elevator is not working again' for things that are broken or fixed. Working is also common before a noun, as in 'a working phone' or 'a working knowledge of Python.' In American English, 'working good' is wrong; say 'working well.'

distinctions.note: Operational is more formal and technical, used in business or engineering reports; working is the everyday word for something that functions.
Functional can mean working as intended, or simply serviceable and not pretty; working is more neutral and everyday.
Workable describes a plan that is practical and could be carried out; working describes something that is currently functioning.

examples.everyday: Is the dishwasher still working, or should we call someone to look at it?
examples.professional: The prototype is working, but the logging still needs cleanup before we deploy it to production.
examples.analytical: A working model of the mind is useful only if it predicts behavior, not if it merely reproduces our intuitions.

nuance.analogy: A working engine is like a heart that keeps beating: nobody notices it until it stops.
nuance.etymology: From the verb work (Old English wyrcan) with the -ing participle ending.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the machine works good' instead of 'works well'; good is an adjective, not an adverb.
Using working as a noun where English needs 'workings' for the internal parts or methods of something.

working.etymology: From Middle English *werking*, *werkynge*, *warkynge*, *worchinge*, from Old English *wyrċing* (“working”), verbal noun of *wyrċan* (“to work”), equivalent to *work* + *ing*.

senses.definition: A room, especially one which is not particularly large, used for manufacturing or other light industrial work.
senses.example: The carpenter kept his tools neatly arranged in the small workshop behind the garage.

senses.definition: A brief, intensive course of education for a small group, emphasizing interaction and practical problem solving.
senses.example: The three-day workshop taught nurses how to lead difficult conversations with anxious patients.

senses.definition: An academic conference.
senses.example: Over two hundred researchers attended the workshop on machine learning fairness last spring.

senses.definition: To help a playwright revise a draft of (a play) by rehearsing it with actors and critiquing the results.
senses.example: The director workshopped the new script with the cast for two weeks before opening night.

senses.definition: To work on or revise something, especially collaboratively, in a workshop.
senses.example: We workshopped the grant proposal in a group session, rewriting weak paragraphs together.

senses.definition: To improve through collaboration.
senses.example: Our team workshopped the dashboard design until every chart felt clear and useful.

core.definition: A short, hands-on session where a small group learns or practices a skill, usually with an instructor and group discussion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WURK, and keep the second syllable light. The vowel in shop is the open /ɑ/ of the cot-caught merger, so it sounds like 'shahp', not 'shop' with a rounded o.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests learning, collaboration, and practical benefit. In a manufacturing or trades context it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use workshop for training sessions at work, schools, and community centers, and for creative writing or art classes; it sounds more practical and hands-on than seminar or lecture. In manufacturing and trades, a workshop is a physical room where things are made or repaired. In theater, to workshop a play means to develop it with actors, and in academic life a workshop can be a small conference on a narrow topic.

distinctions.note: A seminar is usually a discussion-based class or talk on an academic topic; a workshop is more hands-on, with participants practicing a skill.
Training is often required and organized around job performance; a workshop may be voluntary and more exploratory.
A conference is a large event with many talks over several days; a workshop is smaller and more interactive, though academic workshops can be part of a conference.

examples.everyday: My daughter is going to a pottery workshop on Saturday mornings, and she loves it.
examples.professional: I'm running a two-day workshop on data quality for the analytics team next month, so please block the afternoons.
examples.analytical: The workshop model assumes that understanding grows through collaborative critique rather than through the one-way transfer of fixed content.

nuance.analogy: A workshop is like a kitchen where people cook together and taste each other's dishes, rather than a restaurant where a chef serves a finished meal.
nuance.etymology: From work plus shop, originally a place where manual work was done.
common_mistakes: Using workshop to mean any meeting; a workshop should involve practice or making something, not just listening.
Saying 'workshop about' a topic; the usual phrase is 'workshop on,' as in 'a workshop on data privacy.'

senses.definition: An injury, such as a cut, stab, or tear, to a (usually external) part of the body.
senses.example: The nurse cleaned the deep wound on his leg before stitching the cut closed.

senses.definition: A hurt to a person's feelings, reputation, prospects, etc.
senses.example: It took a long time to get over the wound of that insult.

senses.definition: An injury to a person by which the skin is divided or its continuity broken.
senses.example: The stab wound on his arm required six stitches and a tetanus shot.

senses.definition: To hurt or injure (someone) by cutting, piercing, or tearing the skin.
senses.example: The police officer wounded the suspect during the fight that ensued.

senses.definition: To hurt (a person's feelings).
senses.example: The actor's pride was wounded when the leading role went to his rival.

core.definition: An injury to the body, such as a cut, stab, or tear, that breaks the skin or damages tissue.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, 'wound' has a long oo vowel and rhymes with 'moon.' It is not the same as the past tense of 'wind,' which is pronounced 'wowned' with a diphthong. Keep the stress on the single syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes injury or pain, though it can be used figuratively for emotional hurt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wound' in everyday talk about cuts and injuries, such as 'a deep wound on his arm,' and in medical or news contexts. For a small cut, people often say 'cut' or 'scrape' instead. Figurative uses are common in serious conversations, but they can sound dramatic if used for minor problems.

distinctions.note: 'Injury' is a broader term for any harm to the body, while 'wound' specifically means a break in the skin or tissue, often from a weapon or sharp object.
'Cut' is an everyday word for a small opening in the skin, while 'wound' is more formal and often used for serious or deep injuries.

examples.everyday: Hold a clean towel on that wound until the bleeding stops, and then put a bandage on it.
examples.professional: The safety report lists every worker wound from the new equipment, along with the cause of each injury.
examples.analytical: Scripture often uses the image of a wound to describe the damage that sin does to human relationships and the body.

nuance.analogy: Like a crack in a window, a wound breaks the protective surface, and healing is the process of sealing it again.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wund, meaning a physical injury.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the noun 'wound' like the past tense of 'wind' (wowned), which is a different word.
Using 'wound' for a small scrape in everyday talk, where 'cut' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, the most common word for a wound is makkah, meaning a blow or stroke, while the New Testament Greek plēgē means a blow or wound. Isaiah 53:5 (RSV) says that the servant was wounded for human transgressions and bruised for their iniquities, a passage Christians often read as prophecy of Christ. Proverbs 27:6 (RSV) observes that the wounds a friend inflicts are faithful, meaning honest criticism is better than false flattery. Jeremiah 6:14 (RSV) criticizes leaders who lightly heal the wound of the people while falsely promising peace.

wound.etymology: Noun from Middle English *wund*, from Old English *wund*, from **wundu*, from Proto-Germanic **wundō* (“wound”), from Proto-Indo-European **wen-* (“to strive, toil, win”).

senses.definition: Suffering from a wound, especially one acquired in battle from a weapon, such as a gun or a knife.
senses.example: A wounded soldier.

senses.definition: Suffering from an emotional injury.
senses.example: My wounded pride never recovered from her rejection.

senses.definition: Of a particle: having undergone an inelastic collision.
senses.example: a wounded nucleon

core.definition: Injured by a weapon or force, or emotionally hurt by something someone said or did.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WOON, and the ending -ed is a short 'id' sound. Do not pronounce the ending as a separate long 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests suffering, whether physical or emotional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wounded' in news about soldiers or accidents, such as 'a wounded veteran,' and in everyday talk about feelings, such as 'She sounded wounded by his comment.' It is also used as a noun, as in 'the wounded were taken to the hospital.' It can sound dramatic when used for trivial hurts.

distinctions.note: 'Injured' is the everyday word for physical harm from any cause, while 'wounded' suggests a break in the skin, often from a weapon, or a deep emotional hurt.
'Hurt' is the most common and flexible word, while 'wounded' is stronger and more literary.

examples.everyday: My brother still sounds wounded about the way his old boss treated him.
examples.professional: The team is wounded after the reorg, so we need to rebuild trust before the next launch.
examples.analytical: Jesus' description of the wounded traveler in the parable shows that compassion is owed even to a stranger who is injured.

nuance.analogy: Like a bruised apple, the outside looks mostly fine, but the damage underneath is real and needs care.
nuance.etymology: From 'wound' (noun) plus the past participle ending -ed, from Old English wund.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'wun-DID,' instead of 'WOON-did.'
Using 'wounded' for a minor physical scratch, where 'injured' or 'hurt' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: Isaiah 53:5 (RSV) describes the servant as wounded for transgressions and bruised for iniquities, and Christian readers have traditionally connected this to the suffering of Christ. The word appears in the Old Testament Hebrew as a form of the root for wound or pierce, expressing both physical and moral suffering. Scripture also presents the wounded as those who need compassion, as in the story of the Good Samaritan.

senses.definition: Any of various bars to aid with demolition tasks: prybars or crowbars.
senses.example: He pried the rotten boards loose with a wrecking bar during the kitchen demolition.

core.definition: Heavy steel prybar used to pull apart boards, nails, and framing during demolition work.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, Americans put the main stress on WRECK, as in other noun compounds like pickup truck, and give bar only light secondary stress. The -ing ending is a short i sound, and the final r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical tool term used in construction, renovation and demolition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wrecking bar for a flat, heavy prybar with a claw, common in construction and home renovation. In hardware stores you may also hear flat bar or crowbar, and crowbar is the more general everyday word. The term does not refer to vehicles or people, so do not confuse it with wrecker.

distinctions.note: Crowbar is the more common everyday term, and it usually refers to a long pry tool with a curved claw end, though the two words overlap.
Pry bar is a general term for any lever used for prying, while wrecking bar suggests a heavier tool for demolition work.

collocations: pry boards off with a wrecking bar
keep a wrecking bar in the truck

examples.everyday: Hand me the wrecking bar from the truck so I can pull off this old trim before the drywall guys come.
examples.professional: The crew logged the wrecking bars and sledgehammers as tools for the interior demolition phase.
examples.analytical: Historic preservation guidelines usually forbid using a wrecking bar on original plaster, because it destroys the surviving material.

nuance.analogy: A wrecking bar works like a long lever on a stuck rock: a small push at one end pries the whole thing loose.
nuance.etymology: Wrecking is from wreck plus -ing; bar is from Old French barre, a rod or lever.
common_mistakes: Stressing bar instead of WRECK, as in wreck-ING BAR.
Confusing wrecking bar with wrench, which is a tool for turning nuts and bolts.

senses.definition: A measuring stick thirty-six inches (one yard) long.
senses.example: My grandfather kept a worn wooden yardstick hanging by the workbench in his garage.

senses.definition: A standard to which other measurements or comparisons are judged.

core.definition: A standard or measure used to judge, compare, or evaluate other things.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on YARD, and the second word, stick, has a lighter secondary stress. Say 'stik' with a short i, and keep the r in yard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a standard of comparison and can be negative when used to judge someone harshly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'by any yardstick' or 'by that yardstick' to mean 'by any standard' or 'by that measure,' as in 'By any yardstick, this was a successful launch.' It originally meant a literal measuring stick, but in everyday and business talk the figurative sense is far more common. Use it when you are comparing things against a benchmark.

distinctions.note: A benchmark is a reference point or test used to measure performance, often in technical or business settings, while a yardstick is a more general standard for judgment.
A criterion is a formal condition that must be met, whereas a yardstick is a practical measure you compare things against.
A metric is a quantified measurement, while a yardstick is the standard against which measurements or results are judged.

examples.everyday: By my yardstick, a good dinner is one where nobody checks their phone.
examples.professional: We should use last quarter's conversion rate as the yardstick for judging the new campaign.
examples.analytical: Whether a theory is useful is a different yardstick from whether it is true, and philosophers often confuse the two.

nuance.analogy: A yardstick is like a ruler you hold up to everything: it does not change the object, but it lets you compare sizes fairly.
nuance.etymology: From yard (a unit of length) and stick, literally a stick one yard long used for measuring.
common_mistakes: Saying 'yard-stick' with the stress spread evenly; the stress falls clearly on the first word.
Using 'yardstick' as a verb; it is a noun, so say 'use a yardstick' or 'measure by a yardstick'.

core.definition: A personal name in the Hebrew Bible, borne by several men, including an overseer of David's wine cellars and a Benjamite and an Asaphite listed in the genealogies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ZAB, with a short a as in cab. The final syllable is pronounced like the word eye, so it sounds like ZAB-dy.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name in scripture with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Zabdi mainly in Bible study or when reading the Old Testament genealogies and lists of David's officials. It is rare as a modern given name. Readers may confuse it with Zabad, so checking the father's name is helpful.

examples.everyday: When we read 1 Chronicles at church, the pastor pointed out Zabdi, who was in charge of the wine cellars.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan on David's administration, Zabdi appears as an official responsible for storage, so students should note his role.
examples.analytical: The appearance of Zabdi among David's officials shows how the Chronicler records administrative offices alongside family lines.

nuance.analogy: Zabdi is like a name on a company org chart, whose job title tells you what he did in the household of the king.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Zavdi, probably meaning my gift, from a root meaning to bestow.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as dee instead of dy.
Mixing up Zabdi with Zabad, a different name in the same books.
nuance.biblical_note: Zabdi appears in several places. In 1 Chronicles 27:27 he is the Shiphmite who was over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars during David's reign. In 1 Chronicles 8:19 Zabdi is a son of Shimei in the tribe of Benjamin. In Joshua 7:1 Achan is identified as descended from Zabdi through Zerah, a family line that makes Zabdi an ancestor of the man who took devoted things at Jericho.

senses.definition: Energetic and lively.
Quick, speedy.

core.definition: Quick, lively and full of energy; fast, bright or speedy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZIP. The final -y is a long 'ee' sound, not 'eye'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly; it praises speed, energy or brightness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use zippy for something fast, lively or peppy, such as a zippy sports car, a zippy app or a zippy new café. It is informal and positive, so for a formal report say efficient or responsive instead. It can describe people too, but it is more often used for things.

distinctions.note: Energetic describes a person's energy, while zippy also describes things, such as a fast car or responsive software.
Zingy stresses sharp flavor or wit, while zippy stresses quick, lively motion or speed.

examples.everyday: The new coffee shop has zippy service, so I'm in and out in five minutes.
examples.professional: The new version is zippy on large files, so the team will switch over this quarter.
examples.analytical: A zippy argument can persuade quickly, but it often skips the careful qualifications the claim needs.

nuance.analogy: Like a small sports car: bright, nimble and quick off the line.
nuance.etymology: From zip, meaning energy or speed, with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -y as 'eye' instead of 'ee'.
Using zippy for a formal recommendation or reference letter, where it sounds too casual.
Confusing zippy with zippier, the comparative form, and forgetting to change the y to i before -er.
